title: Complex Gender and Microvascular Surgery Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (post-residency plastic surgery); MGB and Johns Hopkins are distinct institutional variants, not a documented combined program.-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Physician-level preparation and completed plastic-surgery residency recommended for the intended learner; this course is not an eligibility pathway.
Working knowledge of plastic-surgery anatomy, wound healing, perioperative risk, reconstructive principles, and evidence-based medicine.
Familiarity with shared decision-making, informed consent, research ethics, and respectful care of transgender and gender-diverse people.
objectives: Describe the official MGB and Johns Hopkins fellowship tracks without conflating them or inferring accreditation/board status.
Compare broad surgical options across chest, facial, genital, and microsurgical reconstruction through patient goals, anatomy, risks, staging, and aftercare.
Appraise relevant primary and guideline sources, identify evidence limits, and distinguish institutional service descriptions from guidelines.
Construct safe multidisciplinary discussion and follow-up frameworks for fictional education cases.
Map knowledge to broad ABPS plastic-surgery written/oral domains while recognizing no separate GAS board examination was identified.
Explain why online self-study cannot confer procedural competence, licensure, case volume, board eligibility, or clinical authorization.

units.title: Scope, terminology, ethics, and evidence literacy
objectives: Distinguish gender identity, gender incongruence, dysphoria, treatment goals, and surgical options without presuming an individual goal.
Use person-first, affirming communication and shared decision-making; identify when evidence or policy is jurisdiction-specific.
topics: Evidence hierarchies, guideline limitations, informed consent, confidentiality, and health equity
boardDomains: ABPS general professional judgment/ethics; not a gender-surgery-specific exam blueprint
casePractice: Compare the official MGB and Hopkins scopes; explain which items are program facts versus consensus guidance.
units.assessment: Short-answer evidence appraisal plus terminology audit.

units.title: Clinical assessment, goals, consent, and individualized planning
objectives: Elicit the person’s own functional, aesthetic, sexual, reproductive, and recovery priorities.
Build a differential/optimization plan without treating identity or mental-health diagnosis as a proxy for capacity.
Discuss consent, alternatives, staged treatment, uncertainty, and follow-up.
boardDomains: ABPS history/physical, patient safety, ethics, judgment
casePractice: Case conference: convert a fictional goal statement into questions for multidisciplinary planning; do not prescribe a procedure.
units.assessment: Viva-style explanation of uncertainties, alternatives, and patient-defined outcomes.

units.title: Applied anatomy and reconstructive/microvascular principles
objectives: Explain high-level vascular, nerve, tissue, donor-site, and recipient-site considerations relevant to reconstructive planning.
Interpret flap survival risks, perfusion monitoring concepts, and the need for supervised procedural training.
boardDomains: ABPS basic science, wound healing, reconstruction, complications
casePractice: Use a schematic (not a patient image) to compare the reasoning variables for a free-tissue reconstruction.
units.assessment: Draw-and-defend reconstruction tradeoff map; no operative skills sign-off.

units.title: Masculinizing chest reconstruction
objectives: Compare common chest-contouring goals and broad technique-selection variables without declaring one technique universally preferred.
Identify counseling domains: scars, sensation, nipple-areola options, revisions, recovery, and complications.
boardDomains: ABPS breast/chest reconstruction, aesthetics, complications, ethics
casePractice: Counsel a fictional patient who prioritizes sensation and minimizes scarring; identify unresolved questions, not a single prescribed operation.
units.assessment: Structured oral defense using goal-concordant outcomes and uncertainty.

units.title: Feminizing chest/breast augmentation
objectives: Describe shared-decision variables for augmentation, implant versus other options, tissue envelope, and patient priorities.
Identify general perioperative counseling and longer-term surveillance questions from current authoritative resources.
boardDomains: ABPS breast, implant safety, patient counseling
casePractice: Create a no-device/no-image consultation checklist that captures goals, alternatives, limitations, and follow-up.
units.assessment: Checklist quality rubric: completeness, neutral language, transparency.

units.title: Facial gender-affirming surgery
objectives: Identify broad categories of facial procedures and the importance of facial analysis, individual goals, and multidisciplinary planning.
Discuss risks, staged planning, and limitations of public educational demonstrations.
topics: Frontal contouring, rhinoplasty, genioplasty/jaw and soft-tissue categories
Goal setting, risk, and outcome measures
boardDomains: ABPS craniofacial/head-neck, aesthetics, ethics, patient safety
casePractice: Analyze a fictional 2-D schematic and propose a shared-decision conference agenda rather than an operative plan.
units.assessment: Blueprint-mapped case presentation; no facial-image diagnosis.

units.title: Feminizing genital reconstruction: vaginoplasty, vulvoplasty, orchiectomy
objectives: Compare the goals and broad options for vaginoplasty and vulvoplasty, including individualized depth goals and postoperative support needs.
Identify anatomy, fertility, urinary/sexual function, and complication domains for counseling.
boardDomains: ABPS genitourinary reconstruction, ethics, complications; no dedicated GAS exam blueprint
casePractice: Fictional case: formulate a question list on depth goals, fertility, recovery, and aftercare without choosing for the patient.
units.assessment: Clinical reasoning rubric: goals, counseling, alternatives, follow-up, uncertainty.

units.title: Masculinizing genital reconstruction: metoidioplasty and phalloplasty
objectives: Differentiate broad reconstructive aims and tradeoffs of metoidioplasty and phalloplasty, including staged and urethral reconstruction considerations.
Explain that outcome priorities and acceptable tradeoffs differ and require individualized counseling.
topics: Phalloplasty tissue-source and staged reconstruction overview
Urethral reconstruction, urinary/sexual goals, and tradeoffs
boardDomains: ABPS genitourinary reconstruction, microsurgery, complication management
casePractice: Use a fictional patient-preference matrix to compare options without ranking them or providing individualized care advice.
units.assessment: Comparative matrix assessed for balance, accuracy, and values alignment.

units.title: Complex revision and non-gender microsurgical urogenital reconstruction
objectives: Identify why prior operations, scar, tissue availability, and referral history change multidisciplinary reconstruction planning.
Recognize boundaries of evidence and the need to seek appropriate expert review.
topics: Communication across plastic surgery, urology, and other teams
boardDomains: ABPS reconstruction, genitourinary, complications, oral judgment
casePractice: Fictional referral handoff: produce a structured summary separating known facts from missing data.
units.assessment: Handoff rubric: safety, uncertainty, differential, escalation, team roles.

units.title: Perioperative medicine, hormones, anesthesia, fertility, and VTE
objectives: Explain why perioperative decisions should use patient-specific risk assessment and current evidence rather than blanket hormone rules.
Identify fertility preservation and medication coordination as time-sensitive shared decisions.
Apply standard VTE prevention principles through institutional clinical protocols, without issuing dosing advice.
topics: VTE risk, prophylaxis individualization, anesthesia, airway and positioning
boardDomains: ABPS perioperative safety, pharmacology, ethics
casePractice: Review a fictional perioperative plan for missing consultations and unsupported blanket assumptions.
units.assessment: Safety audit rubric: individualized risk, evidence quality, coordination, clear caveats.

units.title: Postoperative care, complications, rehabilitation, and continuity
objectives: Build a high-level surveillance/contingency framework for wound, vascular, urinary, pelvic-floor, and functional issues.
Identify follow-up and escalation needs without substituting for local protocols or supervised care.
topics: Dilation/rehabilitation and aftercare as individualized care
boardDomains: ABPS wound care, reconstruction complications, patient safety, oral reasoning
casePractice: Fictional postoperative handoff: list warning features that require urgent clinician evaluation and coordination (no treatment plan).
units.assessment: Handoff assessment: safe triage framing, communication, appropriate escalation.

units.title: Outcomes, quality improvement, scholarship, and board-style synthesis
objectives: Select validated patient-reported and clinical outcomes aligned with the person’s goals.
Interpret limitations of case series/observational evidence and propose a quality-improvement question.
Synthesize broad ABPS plastic-surgery cognition without claiming GAS is a separate board exam.
topics: Outcome constructs and instruments including GENDER-Q
Evidence appraisal, bias, follow-up, and missing data
Written/structured oral synthesis and lifelong learning
boardDomains: ABPS written content outline and oral reasoning; not a specialty-specific board blueprint
casePractice: Draft a one-page QI question using a fictional dataset schema only; no patient-level records.
units.assessment: Capstone rubric: measurable outcome, ethical data handling, limitations, actionability.

assignment.title: Goal-concordant case conference and evidence brief
assignment.description: Using a fictional adult learner vignette (no copied patient case or image), submit (1) a one-page goal and uncertainty map, (2) a multidisciplinary question/referral list, (3) an evidence table with two primary/guideline sources and source dates, (4) a high-level option/tradeoff comparison, and (5) a postoperative follow-up/measurement framework. Do not select a procedure for a real person or include operative instructions.

rubric.criterion: Patient-defined goals, dignity, and shared decision-making
rubric.meets: Goals and values are elicited; language is respectful; no assumptions based on identity.
Claims map to current authoritative sources; distinguishes program descriptions, guidance, and primary evidence; states uncertainty.
Identifies relevant specialties, tradeoffs, risks, fertility/aftercare domains as appropriate; recognizes missing facts and escalation.
Selects goal-aligned measures; maintains privacy and copyright boundaries; no real patient data/images.
Clearly states educational limits; avoids procedural competence/eligibility claims and unsupported universal rules.

assignment.passingRule: Instructor-set formative rubric only; not validated, not an exam predictor, and not a clinical competency assessment.

assessment.format: 10 original multiple-choice items with rationales plus 12 unit exercises and one rubric-scored fictional case-conference assignment.
assessment.boardAlignment: Conceptual alignment to broad ABPS content outline and written cognitive/oral judgment domains. No specialty-specific ABPS blueprint or exam was identified. Questions are original educational items and not official exam content.
assessment.limitations: Not validated, not a board predictor, not patient-care advice, and no procedural or supervised skill assessment.

A complete public MGB or Johns Hopkins lecture catalog and exact didactic-hour ledger were not found. The 36-hour target is therefore infeasible to verify from the accessible free recording set identified here; no planned scripts are represented as rendered hours.

medical.trackType: Clinical physician fellowship (post-residency plastic surgery); MGB and Johns Hopkins are distinct institutional variants, not a documented combined program.
boardNames: American Board of Plastic Surgery (ABPS) — parent specialty certification only; not a fellowship-specific board
medical.boardStatus: ABPS is the relevant parent plastic-surgery certifying board. Official ABPS materials reviewed describe broad plastic-surgery written and oral examinations. No separate gender-affirming surgery/microsurgery board or dedicated fellowship exit exam was identified in the current official sources reviewed; this is a bounded negative finding, not a guarantee that no institution has an internal assessment. ACEPS is a match/educator organization, not a certifying board.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: The MGB program page requires completed plastic-surgery residency. The ACEPS national registry describes participating fellowship applicants as completing an ACGME-accredited plastic surgery residency by the match-cycle cutoff; Hopkins lists Maryland medical-license eligibility. These are program/match-specific prerequisites, not a determination of an individual’s ABPS eligibility. ABPS certification has its own prerequisite training, practice, examination, and case requirements. A fellowship and this independent course do not confer board eligibility.

practiceQuestions.stem: An adult asks about gender-affirming surgery but describes goals that do not map neatly onto one procedure. What is the best next educational reasoning step?

text: Select the most common operation for the person’s gender identity.
Elicit the person’s functional, aesthetic, reproductive, sexual, and recovery priorities and discuss options, alternatives, and uncertainty.
Require a fixed social-transition duration before further discussion.
Defer all care until two independent letters are obtained in every case.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Care should be individualized and goal-concordant; avoid assumptions and universalized prerequisites. SOC8 is an evidence-based framework, while eligibility and local policy must be verified separately. [7]

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the MGB Complex Gender and Microvascular Surgery Fellowship?

text: It is a board-certified specialty with an independent final examination.
It is a physician fellowship in MGB plastic surgery; the official page requires completion of plastic surgery residency and describes an apprenticeship model.
It is a two-year ACGME residency in urology.
It guarantees ABPS board eligibility after completion.

practiceQuestions.rationale: MGB identifies the post-residency fellowship and plastic surgery residency prerequisite. Neither its page nor the ABPS source establishes a separate GAS board or automatic board eligibility. [1] [4]

practiceQuestions.stem: A trainee is asked whether ABPS offers a distinct gender-affirming surgery certification examination. Which answer is best supported by the reviewed official material?

text: Yes; every GAS fellow must pass a dedicated ABPS GAS exam.
The ABPS publishes broad plastic-surgery written/oral examinations; no separate GAS-specific board examination was identified in the reviewed official material.
ACEPS match completion itself confers ABPS certification.
All graduates of any GAS fellowship automatically earn a plastic surgery certificate.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABPS materials describe broad plastic surgery examination pathways. ACEPS is a fellowship match/educator organization, not a certifying board. The conclusion is bounded to sources reviewed. [4] [6] [3]

practiceQuestions.stem: Which description of MGB and Johns Hopkins is accurate?

text: One combined cross-institutional program with a shared curriculum is officially documented.
Two distinct institutional fellowship variants are publicly listed; the pages describe overlapping subject matter but do not establish a shared curriculum.
Hopkins only offers a research postdoc.
The MGB listing is a generic directory category without a program page.

practiceQuestions.rationale: MGB and Hopkins maintain separate program pages, and ACEPS registry lists both. Programmatically they are variants, not proof of a joint curriculum. [1] [2] [3]

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient’s surgical goals do not include creation of a vaginal canal. Which learning principle should guide the case discussion?

text: Discuss individualized options, including procedures with or without canal creation, and the aftercare implications in light of that person’s goals.
Treat vulvoplasty and vaginoplasty as identical procedures.

practiceQuestions.rationale: UCLA describes vaginoplasty with or without a vaginal cavity, based on preference; local offerings are not a universal standard. [7] [9]

practiceQuestions.stem: When discussing phalloplasty, which counseling frame best reflects available institutional patient information?

text: It is always a single-stage procedure with a predictable result.
It may be multistage; tissue source, urinary passage reconstruction, staging, donor-site issues, and individual goals need discussion.
Every patient must choose the same donor site.
Postoperative follow-up is unnecessary after discharge.

practiceQuestions.rationale: UCLA describes phalloplasty as multistage and notes tissue may come from different donor sites with later stages in some plans; actual decisions require the patient’s clinical team. [9]

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best handles perioperative estrogen management in a fictional patient with thromboembolic risk factors?

text: Every patient must stop all hormones for exactly four weeks.
Continue or stop automatically, without considering context.
Use individualized risk assessment and discuss decisions with the patient and relevant prescribing/surgical/anesthesia clinicians; evidence is limited and protocols vary.
Ignore VTE prevention because gender-affirming surgery has no thrombotic risk.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The open perioperative review describes limited/heterogeneous evidence and notes individualized shared decisions; current practice must also follow contemporary guidance and local protocols. [11] [7]

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner finds a public institutional video of surgery and wants to place screenshots in a new course deck. What is the best action?

text: Copy images because free viewing means reuse rights.
Link to the original and do not copy or redistribute without explicit permission; assess any patient-consent/de-identification status rather than assuming it.
Remove the source logo and republish.
Assume all surgical media are synthetic.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Public view access is not reuse permission; UCSF terms expressly restrict copying/republication absent permission. The UCLA and ASPS pages provide hosted viewing, not an explicit republication license. [13] [9] [17]

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the most appropriate use of GENDER-Q in this course?

text: Treat it as an operative eligibility test.
Treat it as an outcome-measure resource; do not infer access to patient-level cases or use it to substitute for clinical assessment.
Treat it as proof that all procedures have equal outcomes.
Use it to guarantee postoperative satisfaction.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Brigham’s PROVE Center describes GENDER-Q as a patient-reported outcome measure. Outcome tools support measurement; they do not confer eligibility or guarantee outcomes. [18]

practiceQuestions.stem: A public fellowship page says the fellow is expected to graduate with microsurgical proficiency. What does this establish for an independent online course learner?

text: That watching a lecture establishes operative competence.
That the official program describes supervised fellowship learning; an online course cannot supply procedural competence, supervision, licensure, or case volume.
That all trainees can perform independent microsurgery at enrollment.
That completion yields a separate board certificate.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Hopkins describes a 12-month intensive rotation and expected graduate proficiency; the official program context is supervised clinical training, which this self-study course cannot reproduce. [2]

title: Brachytherapy Fellowship
prerequisites: Advanced physician learner: completed or near-complete radiation oncology residency or equivalent clinical foundation; programme-specific eligibility is not fully published on the BWH page and must be confirmed directly.
Foundational radiation oncology, oncology, anatomy, radiobiology, medical physics, imaging, and evidence-appraisal knowledge.
This self-study course is independent and does not confer clinical privileges, procedural competence, licensure, radiation-safety authorization, ABR board eligibility, or certification.
objectives: Explain the clinical rationale and limits of brachytherapy within multidisciplinary radiation oncology.
Compare brachytherapy forms, isotopes, dose calculations, clinical contexts, and evidence quality.
Interpret cervical and prostate brachytherapy literature, image-guided workflows, planning concepts, and target/OAR trade-offs.
Recognize quality assurance and radiation-safety concepts requiring trained, licensed multidisciplinary teams.
Use ABR Radiation Oncology physics, biology, clinical and oral-case domains to structure self-study without claiming specialty-exam readiness.
Critically appraise date-sensitive evidence and distinguish official program facts, accreditation requirements, board requirements, and educational resources.

assignment.title: Source-graded brachytherapy case conference memo
assignment.instructions: Choose a publicly accessible, published de-identified source case (or write a clearly fictional vignette). Submit 1,200–1,800 words plus a source map: describe disease context; compare plausible modality options; explain the role/limitations of brachytherapy; identify imaging, target, OAR and safety considerations; discuss uncertainty, patient goals, consent and follow-up; and state what must be confirmed by a qualified clinical team. Do not supply patient-specific treatment advice, procedural steps, prescription or dose. Do not copy, rehost or upload case images or records.

topicGaps: 36 verified free public recording hours are not feasible from the reviewed source set: only 1.9558 h has exact observed durations; 34.0442 h remains unfilled. Existing target minutes and unrendered clip plans are not runtime evidence.

topicGaps: 36 verified free public recording hours are not feasible from the reviewed source set: only 1.9558 h has exact observed durations; 34.0442 h remains unfilled. Existing target minutes and unrendered clip plans are not runtime evidence.

Public free recordings now directly cover an HDR radiation safety/emergency session and one short ABS hybrid-applicator webinar. Runtime, access, and expert scope vary; no whole playlist length is inferred.

No verified full-length, open, runtime-observed recording was located for cervical imaging-based target/OAR planning, prostate LDR comparison, other anatomic-site indications, cumulative EQD2/BED application, or systematic evidence appraisal; authored scripts teach selected concepts but do not fill video hours.
AAPM MPPG 13.a detailed full text remained inaccessible through PMC automated challenge during this review; official AAPM page confirms its scope but not all detailed recommendations.

BWH official fellowship page remains contact-only for rotations, eligibility details, case minima, and didactic hours. Dana-Farber page describes the 12-month full-time clinical fellowship and clinical-research component but not its detailed timetable or accreditation.

Prostate sources include a 2018 open review with historical regimen claims; those claims are not treatment recommendations. AUA/ASTRO 2026 page exposes summary/access notices but its detailed guideline is login-restricted; no login or bypass was attempted.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best characterizes the BWH/Dana-Farber brachytherapy fellowship evidence?

options.text: Public pages establish an ACGME-accredited brachytherapy residency with fixed case minimums.

The institutional listing is a clinical physician fellowship; Dana-Farber describes a 12-month full-time clinically focused fellowship with a clinical research component, but published detailed rotations/case minimums are not available.
The program is research-only and for non-physicians.
Completing it guarantees ABR subspecialty eligibility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The Dana-Farber radiation oncology training page distinguishes its clinical brachytherapy fellowship (12 months, full-time, clinically focused plus clinical research) from medical-physics training. The BWH page currently gives contact information only; neither page establishes accreditation or case thresholds.

ABR Radiation Oncology certification process, including its Qualifying and Oral Certifying examinations
ACGME brachytherapy board
ABS licensing exam

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABR describes RO certification exams and eligibility. Its current subspecialty listing identifies pain medicine for radiation oncology, not brachytherapy; ABS is a specialty society, not a licensing/board body.

practiceQuestions.stem: For definitive treatment of locally advanced cervical carcinoma, what is the ABS consensus position at a high level?

options.text: Brachytherapy is generally replaced by external beam dose escalation.
Brachytherapy is strongly recommended as a component of definitive treatment; case-specific technique and current guidance still matter.
All cases should use a single applicator and fractionation.
Brachytherapy can be omitted if MRI is available.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABS consensus guideline abstract recommends brachytherapy as a component of definitive treatment for locally advanced cervical carcinoma. It does not imply identical technique, dose, or eligibility for every patient.

practiceQuestions.stem: When might hybrid intracavitary/interstitial cervical brachytherapy be evaluated?

options.text: Whenever MRI is unavailable, by default.
When acceptable target coverage cannot be achieved with intracavitary treatment alone or nearby OAR dose is too high, among other selected anatomic situations.
For every cervical cancer independent of anatomy.
Only for prostate tumors.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The reviewed hybrid guide identifies inadequate target coverage/OAR concerns and selected bulky, asymmetric, parametrial, or vaginal extension scenarios as contexts for evaluation, not a universal indication.

It certifies procedural competence.

practiceQuestions.stem: A published 2023 hybrid cervical brachytherapy guide supports which approach?

options.text: Treat its illustrative patient images as downloadable public-domain content.
Use the article for conceptual learning; images remain subject to article copyright/license and should not be copied/rehosted without permission.
Its workflow replaces supervised training.
Hybrid implants are automatically superior in all cases.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is a correct conceptual property of HDR brachytherapy?

options.text: Source geometry and dwell positions/times can strongly shape dose, so applicator reconstruction and delivery QA are safety-critical.
Dose is independent of applicator position.
HDR never requires a radioactive materials license.
One DVH metric alone proves clinical benefit.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABR physics domain includes brachytherapy, planning, QA and safety. AAPM practice guidance emphasizes quality standards and safety in HDR workflows; planning metrics need clinical context.
practiceQuestions.domain: Brachytherapy fellowship knowledge; underlying ABR Radiation Oncology physics/biology/clinical domains

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about TG-43-style dose calculations is most appropriate for learners?

options.text: They remove the need for independent planning checks.
Treat the formalism and its assumptions as a physics framework; source, geometry, tissue heterogeneity, applicator and model limits require qualified review.
It is a surgical staging system.
It determines ABR eligibility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABR includes brachytherapy and treatment-planning physics. Learners should understand model assumptions, not infer safety or eligibility from a dose formalism alone.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner encounters a video about a historic prostate HDR fractionation regimen. What is the best response?

options.text: Treat it as current universal clinical instruction.
Check current disease-specific guidance, evidence, patient context, and institutional protocols; do not reuse a historical regimen as a prescription.
Ignore tumor risk and urinary function.
Use the video as board certification.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Clinical regimens and indications change and are patient-specific. The ABR describes board content, while specialty guidelines and current treating-team protocols govern clinical practice.
practiceQuestions.domain: Brachytherapy fellowship knowledge; underlying ABR Radiation Oncology physics/biology/clinical domains

practiceQuestions.stem: Which limitation applies to this independent self-study course?

options.text: Completion qualifies learners for a medical license.
Completion certifies competence for implant placement.
It does not replace accredited clinical training, supervised procedures, licensure, radiation-safety authorization, board eligibility, or certification.
It guarantees a passing board score.

practiceQuestions.rationale: These are explicit course boundaries; the ABR certification pathway requires qualifying education/training and examinations; an independent curriculum confers none of these.

unitMap.text: Role, scope and goal-concordant palliation
coveredTopics: Differentiate symptom palliation, durable local control, emergency stabilization and treatment intent without assuming these goals are mutually exclusive.
Frame intervention burden, prognosis uncertainty, patient values and alternatives in shared decision-making.
Describe which claims belong to institutional fellowship descriptions, board policies or guidelines.

unitMap.text: Symptom assessment, pain mechanisms and analgesic integration
coveredTopics: Use a structured pain history and distinguish nociceptive, neuropathic, incident and treatment-related pain.
Identify when radiotherapy is one component rather than a substitute for analgesia, urgent workup or multidisciplinary care.
Explain response assessment and pain flare as possible post-RT phenomena.

unitMap.text: Bone metastases: candidacy and treatment selection
coveredTopics: Separate uncomplicated painful lesions from instability, impending fracture, cord compression and postoperative situations.
Compare patient-specific tradeoffs among conventional EBRT, SBRT, surgery, systemic/bone-modifying treatments and observation.
Interpret the uncertainty and endpoints of comparative effectiveness evidence; avoid a universal fractionation rule.

unitMap.text: Spinal metastases and MSCC emergency pathways
coveredTopics: Recognize red-flag neurologic and pain presentations that require urgent escalation.
Summarize the NICE pathway for imaging, stabilization, surgery/radiotherapy and supportive care, adapting to local jurisdiction.
Identify why anatomy, instability, neurologic function, prior RT and histology alter multidisciplinary planning.

unitMap.text: Brain metastases and neurologic symptom palliation
coveredTopics: Compare decision variables for SRS, fractionated SRS, WBRT approaches, systemic therapy, surgery and supportive care.
Use functional status, lesion burden/size/location, prognosis, prior cranial RT, cognition and patient preferences in framing decisions.
Distinguish guideline recommendations from local practice and evolving CNS-active systemic therapy evidence.

unitMap.text: Thoracic symptoms: dyspnea, cough, hemoptysis, obstruction
coveredTopics: Construct a differential for dyspnea and identify time-critical causes needing non-radiation intervention.
Summarize palliative thoracic RT evidence while noticing that the ASTRO NSCLC guideline update is from 2018.
Set expectations about time to benefit, symptom control and acute toxicity without presenting a fractionation recipe.

unitMap.text: Bleeding and other focal symptoms
coveredTopics: Assess acuity, hemodynamic risk, source, goals and parallel urgent stabilization before considering hemostatic RT.
Describe symptom-specific evidence limitations for bleeding, obstruction and painful soft-tissue disease.
Plan measures for concurrent analgesia, wound care and reassessment with the treating team.

unitMap.text: Reirradiation, cumulative dose and safety reasoning
coveredTopics: Reconstruct prior fields, prescription, fractionation, interval and organs-at-risk dose before considering overlap.
Explain BED/EQD2 as model-based comparison tools with assumptions and uncertainty rather than a permission threshold.
Escalate complex retreatment to experienced radiation oncology/physics review; this course grants no planning authority.

unitMap.text: Treatment burden, planning and care coordination
coveredTopics: Map referral, decision, simulation, immobilization, planning, QA, delivery, symptom support and follow-up as a service pathway.
Identify barriers including travel, positioning, transportation, caregiver burden, access, cost and scheduling.
Use simplest appropriate workflow without compromising safety, diagnostic confidence or established QA.

unitMap.text: Communication, uncertainty, consent and serious illness conversations
coveredTopics: Practice eliciting desired information, values and decision roles.
Communicate prognosis and treatment trade-offs using calibrated uncertainty and teach-back.
Recognize when symptom complexity, existential distress, caregiver needs or goals warrant specialist palliative care.

unitMap.text: Toxicity prevention, response and follow-up
coveredTopics: Anticipate site-specific acute and late toxicity, competing risks and symptom flare.
Define a follow-up plan that checks the patient-reported outcome most relevant to the treatment goal.
Distinguish urgent adverse-event triage from routine post-treatment reassessment.

unitMap.text: Evidence, ethics, equity and reflective practice
coveredTopics: Appraise guideline date, population, outcome, certainty, generalizability and potential competing interests.
Apply an equity lens to access and treatment burden while avoiding unsupported utilization benchmarks.
Present a defensible recommendation and explicit uncertainty to a multidisciplinary case conference.

Unit 1: authored introduction only; lacks recorded source lectures and comprehensive parent-specialty or palliative medicine domains.

Unit 3: one planning webinar plus authored bone-evidence lesson; no full disease-specific curriculum, stability assessment instruction, or treatment planning credential.
Unit 4: one planning webinar plus authored MSCC escalation lesson; no full clinical emergency training or image interpretation.
Unit 5: authored brain-metastasis decision lesson; no verified recording and no current histology-specific clinical pathway or planning instruction.

Unit 7: no verified recording or authored full episode yet; evidence for bleeding, obstruction and focal soft-tissue symptoms remains insufficiently mapped to specific contemporary primary guideline sources.

Unit 10: no verified recording; communication PDQ is an informational source, not supervised serious-illness conversation practice.
Unit 11: no verified recording or authored full episode; toxicity and follow-up remain site-specific and incompletely supported by public source material.
Unit 12: no verified recording or authored full episode; evidence/ethics/equity need broader peer-reviewed source mapping and qualified faculty review.

medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with painful radiographically confirmed bone metastasis asks whether one schedule is always best. What is the most defensible teaching response?

options.text: A single fraction is always equivalent in all clinical settings and never requires retreatment.
Choice is contextual: symptom, prognosis, lesion stability, prior RT, goals, burden and available alternatives matter; guidelines and comparative evidence must be applied to the case.
SBRT should be used for all symptomatic bone lesions.
Radiation replaces analgesia after referral.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASTRO 2024 provides evidence-informed options but not a single universal schedule. AHRQ found broadly similar longer-term pain response for single- and multifraction conventional EBRT in uncomplicated disease, with evidence limits and differing retreatment rates; complexity, goals and other modalities affect selection. This is educational, not a prescription.

practiceQuestions.stem: A person with known cancer reports new severe axial back pain and progressive leg weakness. What should an educational pathway prioritize?

options.text: Routine follow-up after the next oncology visit.
Urgent assessment and escalation for possible MSCC, including prompt imaging and multidisciplinary review under local emergency pathways.
Empiric palliative RT without reviewing imaging.
Wait to see whether analgesics resolve the weakness.

practiceQuestions.rationale: New neurologic deficit with cancer and severe spinal pain is an emergency pattern. NICE NG234 covers recognition, urgent investigation, stability assessment, radiotherapy and invasive intervention. The exact steps depend on local pathways; neither this answer nor a course authorizes treatment.

practiceQuestions.stem: In an MSCC case discussion, which missing information most directly undermines safe reirradiation reasoning?

options.text: Prior RT fields, dose/fractionation, dates and relevant organ-at-risk exposure.
Favorite treatment machine brand.
Whether the patient watched an online lecture.
The color scale on a screenshot.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Reirradiation requires reconstruction of prior exposure and overlap, followed by expert multidisciplinary and physics review. BED/EQD2 calculations are model dependent and do not replace case-specific judgment or validated limits.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with several intact brain metastases has good functional status and asks about options. Which statement best reflects current guideline reasoning?

options.text: There is one modality that is best for every patient regardless of lesion number, size, cognition or systemic therapy.
Options can include SRS, fractionated SRS, WBRT strategies, surgery, CNS-active systemic therapy or supportive care; selection depends on clinical and patient-specific factors.
Supportive care is contraindicated when brain metastases are present.
Imaging follow-up is never appropriate.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASTRO 2022 addresses intact and resected metastases and discusses SRS, HA-WBRT, systemic therapy and circumstances to defer RT in favor of supportive care or surveillance. The recommendation is not one-size-fits-all.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient has advanced lung cancer and new breathlessness. What is the safest first reasoning step before assuming tumor-related dyspnea should be treated with RT?

options.text: Assess urgency and differential causes, recognizing dyspnea is subjective and often multifactorial.
Assume airway obstruction in every case.
Offer thoracic RT before clinical assessment.
Ignore possible cardiopulmonary syndromes.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCI PDQ explains dyspnea is multifactorial and describes syndromes including pleural/pericardial effusions, SVC syndrome and lymphangitic carcinomatosis. Urgent stabilization and cause-directed workup can take priority over RT.

practiceQuestions.stem: During counseling for palliative RT, which communication move best supports goal-concordant shared decisions?

options.text: State that symptom relief is guaranteed.
Ask what matters most, explain likely benefits and burdens with uncertainty, invite questions, and check understanding.
Avoid discussing prognosis or alternatives.
Make the decision before asking about patient preferences.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCI communication guidance emphasizes understanding preferences, discussing options and prognosis, supporting trust and quality of life. Good counseling avoids guarantees and makes space for patient values and uncertainty.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner cites ASTRO's 2018 palliative NSCLC guideline as the sole current authority for every thoracic symptom. What is the best critique?

options.text: Its date and defined scope should be made explicit; subsequent evidence and current multidisciplinary guidance should be checked before applying it.
An older guideline is always more accurate.
Guidelines apply identically to all cancer histologies and symptoms.
The date is irrelevant.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ASTRO guideline page identifies the 2018 update and its scope; date-checking and population fit are essential. Avoid extrapolating a guideline beyond its question or assuming that a selected guideline remains the only current authority.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient experiences transient worsening of pain after bone-directed radiotherapy. Which concept should be included in a supportive-care review?

options.text: Pain flare is a possible adverse effect; symptom management and follow-up should be coordinated with the treating team.
It proves local progression.
It proves radiation was ineffective.
It requires no assessment.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCI Cancer Pain PDQ describes radiation-associated pain flare and supportive management evidence. Worsening pain should be assessed in context rather than interpreted as proof of one diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: An educational resource page labels a hospital offering a fellowship. What can that alone establish?

options.text: That a public institutional directory lists an offering under a fellowship label; it does not establish physician-only eligibility, ACGME accreditation or board eligibility.
That the fellowship is ACGME-accredited.
That completion makes every learner board-eligible.
That a public curriculum and rotation schedule exist.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The MGB page provides only its title and contact information, while the discovery source is a directory listing. The public materials reviewed do not disclose eligibility or accreditation; these cannot be inferred.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately distinguishes this institutional fellowship label from board certification?

options.text: ABR lists a distinct supportive/palliative radiation oncology board exam.

ABR certifies radiation oncology as the parent specialty and lists Pain Medicine as an RO subspecialty; separate HPM certification exists through the ABMS-board pathway, but it is not an exam for this named fellowship.
The MGB page guarantees ABIM HPM eligibility.
No board exam exists in radiation oncology.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABR lists radiation oncology initial certification and a Pain Medicine subspecialty; it says it no longer offers HPM certification. ABIM documents a separate HPM exam and training pathway for eligible physicians, including ABR diplomates, which must not be conflated with palliative-radiation training.

Discuss patient identification, consent, peer review, timeouts, image fusion QA and incident learning.
Explain privacy and radiation-safety boundaries for learners.
topics: Target verification; end-to-end QA concepts; peer review; treatment record; consent; human factors; reporting; applicable institutional authorization.
boardDomains: Patient/personnel safety; QA; bioethics; professional conduct
casePractice: Run tabletop failure-mode analysis on a fictional workflow; do not perform or simulate actual treatment.
units.assessment: FMEA rubric: hazard identification 30%, mitigation 30%, escalation/reporting 20%, scope limits 20%.

units.title: Evidence appraisal, board cognition and case synthesis
objectives: Map a clinical vignette to ABR domains: pathology, staging, alternatives, RT technique, dose constraints, safety and follow-up.
Critically appraise guideline quality, evidence strength, generalizability and publication dates.
Communicate a concise oral-board style answer that acknowledges uncertainty.
topics: ABR CNS exam category and overall clinical reasoning; study design; endpoints; absolute vs relative risks; practice questions; no exam prediction.
boardDomains: ABR clinical blueprint; evidence-based treatment; biostatistics; non-clinical skills
casePractice: Present a 5-minute structured answer for fictional case and defend the limitations of available evidence.
units.assessment: Oral rubric: structured response 25%, evidence 25%, alternatives 20%, safety and uncertainty 20%, communication 10%.

assignment.title: Fictional CNS multidisciplinary case conference
assignment.description: Select one scenario from public guideline cases or use a clearly fictional written vignette. Submit a 1,000–1,500-word structured reasoning note, one-page alternative-management matrix, imaging interpretation checklist using lawfully linked case material, and five-minute oral synthesis. No real patient data, images copied from a site, treatment plan, individualized dose or procedural instruction.

rubric.criterion: Alternatives, harms, prognosis and patient values
Imaging, normal tissue and follow-up uncertainty
Safety, ethics, privacy and scope limits

assignment.privacy: Use fictional case facts or linked, authentic teaching cases under their terms. Never include identifiable patient data, copied images or patient records.

assessment.method: Eight to twelve original knowledge questions, twelve unit checks, a fictional case conference and oral synthesis. Suggested self-study completion standard: 80% on knowledge questions and “meets” on each safety/privacy rubric line; this is a course-design threshold only.
assessment.limitations: Questions are original educational items, not validated board questions or a pass predictor. No examination result, clinical competence, certification or guarantee of passing any board is supplied.

studyHours.unitsAndPace: A suggested 12-week plan of about six hours per week. Study hours are a learner workload plan, not verified lecture hours or clinical training.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult with newly diagnosed, neurologically symptomatic brain metastases is eligible for local therapy and also has a CNS-active systemic option. Which approach best reflects the ASTRO recommendation?

options.text: Defer all local treatment because systemic therapy is CNS-active
Recommend upfront local therapy, with multidisciplinary coordination
Give WBRT automatically to every patient
Choose SRS solely by lesion count, ignoring symptoms and context

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASTRO strongly recommends upfront local therapy for symptomatic brain metastases in patients who are candidates, even when CNS-active systemic therapy is available; exact local modality depends on clinical circumstances.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has one intact brain metastasis measuring 1.4 cm, ECOG 1, and a reasonable prognosis. Which is the most accurate guideline-level statement?

options.text: SRS alone is a guideline-supported option; this does not dictate a patient-specific prescription
WBRT is mandatory because all intracranial disease is microscopic
A single-fraction dose can be derived from the ABR examination category
Observation is always equivalent to local treatment

practiceQuestions.rationale: Guidelines support SRS for selected patients with limited intact metastases and reasonable performance status; the appropriate technique and dose require full clinical review and current protocol.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional intact brain metastasis exceeds 4 cm. What is the best general statement consistent with ASTRO guidance?

options.text: Single-fraction SRS is always preferred
Surgery is conditionally recommended; if infeasible, multifraction SRS is preferred over single-fraction SRS
WBRT is prohibited
A historical RTOG table supplies a universal prescription

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASTRO conditionally recommends surgery for lesions over 4 cm; if surgery is not feasible, multifraction SRS is preferred to single-fraction SRS. Patient-specific evaluation remains necessary.

practiceQuestions.stem: Why might omission of WBRT after focal therapy require reliable MRI surveillance and a salvage plan?

options.text: Focal therapy does not prevent distant intracranial recurrence
SRS removes occult metastases throughout the brain
Surveillance substitutes for treatment in all patients
WBRT never improves intracranial control

practiceQuestions.rationale: Local treatments do not control distant intracranial recurrences; close follow-up and access to salvage treatment inform selection. WBRT can improve intracranial control but adds cognitive/toxicity tradeoffs.

practiceQuestions.stem: A post-SRS lesion enlarges on MRI. What is the most defensible next interpretive step?

options.text: Declare radionecrosis based on enhancement alone
Declare tumor recurrence based on size alone
Construct a differential including tumor progression and treatment effect, integrate serial imaging and clinical context
Assume all enlargement is pseudoprogression

practiceQuestions.rationale: Conventional MRI findings can overlap. Follow-up trajectory, advanced imaging, original diagnosis, treatment plan, symptoms and multidisciplinary review contribute; no single imaging sign here establishes the diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which ABR initial Radiation Oncology examination structure is currently described on the official board page?

options.text: Only an SRS oral exam
Qualifying examination with physics, radiation/cancer biology and clinical RO parts, followed by an oral certifying exam
A fellowship attendance test
A CNS-only neuroradiology image exam

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABR lists a qualifying exam consisting of physics, biology and clinical RO parts, and an oral certifying exam. Fellowship completion alone is not this certification pathway.

practiceQuestions.stem: A trainee asks whether Adult CNS Radiosurgery/Radiotherapy has its own ABR board exam. Which response is supported by the current ABR subspecialty page?

options.text: Yes, a CNS SRS subspecialty exam is listed
No separate CNS radiosurgery/SRS ABR exam is listed; ABR offers RO certification and lists pain medicine as its RO subspecialty
All fellowship programmes issue board certificates
ACGME accreditation itself is a board exam

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABR subspecialty page lists pain medicine for radiation oncology, with no CNS radiosurgery/SRS subspecialty exam. This is a date-checked listing, not a claim that no other credential outside ABR exists.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement is best when using the classic RTOG 90-05 dose-escalation report for learning?

options.text: Treat its doses as current universal clinical instructions
Recognize it as a historical study in previously irradiated recurrent tumors and metastases, and check its population, endpoints and limits
Use it instead of contemporary ASTRO guidance
Apply its result to all benign and malignant CNS targets

practiceQuestions.rationale: The PubMed abstract reports a historical cohort/trial context of recurrent previously irradiated lesions, size-associated toxicity and disease-specific outcomes; it cannot stand alone as a contemporary prescription guide.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the listed BWH training offering from ABR certification?

options.text: The BWH listing proves ACGME accreditation and board eligibility
The official page labels it a fellowship under Cancer Institute/Radiology but does not publish detailed eligibility, curriculum or an SRS board credential
The programme is a generic video course
A public listing guarantees state licensure

practiceQuestions.rationale: The BWH page identifies a fellowship listing and contact details, but it does not publish the claimed accreditation, curriculum or eligibility. ABR residency and certification requirements are separate.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about a public TCIA Gamma Knife dataset is correct for a teaching assignment?

options.text: Copy images and patient records into a slide deck because the data are public
Use the linked dataset description; any lawful access must follow NIH controlled-data rules, TCIA terms and required citation, and do not redistribute records
Assume anonymized data are impossible to re-identify
Treat the dataset outcome labels as universal diagnostic truth

practiceQuestions.rationale: The TCIA page reports anonymization and notes that some data potentially suitable for face reconstruction are subject to controlled-access policy; dataset use and citation restrictions still apply. The learning task should not copy or redistribute records/images.

title: HIV Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship track within an infectious diseases fellowship; not a standalone ACGME HIV subspecialty-aligned independent study

prerequisites.level: Advanced physician self-study for ID fellows, infectious-disease clinicians, and other licensed physicians with prior internal-medicine/primary-care foundations; not a beginner course.
requiredKnowledge: Internal medicine and infectious diseases fundamentals
Microbiology, immunology, pharmacology and laboratory interpretation
prerequisites.scopeNote: Students without clinical training may use the materials for general education only. No clinical decisions, prescribing, procedures, diagnosis, or patient management are authorized by course completion.

objectives: Interpret HIV screening and diagnostic testing, including acute infection, HIV-1/HIV-2 differentiation, and discordant results, using current public guidance.
Synthesize baseline assessment and a shared-decision ART plan using current NIH guidance, comorbidities, pregnancy considerations, resistance, drug interactions, and access barriers.
Recognize virologic non-suppression and treatment failure, structure a differential, and identify evidence and specialist resources needed before changing therapy.
Apply guideline-based reasoning to opportunistic infection prevention and treatment, TB, viral hepatitis, STIs, and HIV-associated malignancy without relying on memorized, outdated thresholds.
Integrate prevention including PrEP, PEP, perinatal prevention, and treatment-as-prevention while preserving current eligibility/testing safeguards.
Construct longitudinal primary care plans that address vaccination, cancer screening, cardiovascular/bone/metabolic/mental health, aging, and polypharmacy.
Use trauma-informed, culturally humble, gender-affirming, stigma-aware communication and shared decision-making.
Analyze confidentiality, public-health reporting, health-equity, access, and team-care questions with local-law and guideline caveats.
Use clinical cases, current sources, and uncertainty statements to justify decisions; distinguish educational vignettes from actual patient care.

assignment.name: Longitudinal HIV case synthesis and teaching brief
assignment.instructions: Prepare a 1,500–2,000 word analysis of a wholly fictional or properly sourced public educational case. Address testing/diagnostic reasoning, ART and interactions, OI/co-infection assessment, prevention and primary care, equity/access, follow-up, and uncertainty. Cite current primary guidelines by section and access date. Do not reproduce protected material or use real patient records/images. The assignment is educational and not a clinical plan.

Clearly separates learning from clinical care; lawfully sourced materials

medical.programmeSourceScope: The item packet identifies the official MGB GME listing. Full stateless fetch of that entry displayed only the name and contact. The official MGB ID fellowship pages (fetched 2026-10-07) describe the substantive institutional offering as an HIV Clinician Educator differentiated training track at both MGH and BWH, generally a one-year second-year ID fellowship track, with one HIV position at each site per year. ACGME's 2026 ID requirements specify longitudinal HIV ambulatory experience, including at least 12 months assigned to an HIV clinic under an experienced physician; this is the ID fellowship program requirement, not evidence of a separate HIV accreditation or equivalence between this self-study course and supervised clinical training. No public week-by-week MGB HIV syllabus or full lecture catalogue was found. The similar HIVMA/IDSA Foundation one-year fellowship for non-ID physicians is a distinct national program and was sunset after 2024; the final fellow completed training June 2025. No research-only or non-physician directory categories are included here.
sourceCaveats: Human clinical review has not been performed. Clinical sources and recommendations change; re-open the current guideline chapters before any clinical use.

No stateless playback/login bypass was attempted. Public NIH pages and search metadata were inspected; available page text did not expose a runtime or confirm playback. Both candidate videos therefore have null observed media duration and contribute zero verified hours.

MGB's sparse GME listing and its separate ID programme site use different levels of detail; the distinction between generic directory label and the described MGH/BWH clinician-educator track is preserved.
The MGB webpage reports institutional opportunities and structure, not a public syllabus, actual case counts, individual fellow competence, or personal board eligibility.
The practice questions and scenarios are original educational items, not official or leaked exam content. They do not predict passing or clinical performance.

Free-to-view resource access is not a blanket license to copy, rehost, or reuse images. No patient records or images were copied. Case resources are links; provenance of any source-case de-identification was not independently validated.

This independent educational program has no Harvard/MGB/Johns Hopkins/ABIM/ACGME affiliation or accreditation and does not replace medical school, residency/fellowship, supervised practice, licensure, board eligibility, procedure competence, or certification.

practiceQuestions.stem: A routine HIV screening test is reactive, but the next assay in the current diagnostic sequence is nonreactive or indeterminate. What is the best educational next step?

options.text: Diagnose HIV based on the screening assay alone.
Follow the current supplemental diagnostic algorithm, including nucleic-acid testing when indicated, and arrange appropriate follow-up.
Repeat only the same screening assay in one year.
Assume a false positive and close the evaluation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A reactive screen requires the recommended supplemental sequence; a discordant pattern should not be resolved by unsupported assumption. Recent exposure or acute symptoms can require additional testing. CDC describes assay types and window periods; follow the current diagnostic algorithm and local laboratory advice.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with a possible recent exposure has a negative antibody-only test and compatible acute symptoms. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: The test excludes infection regardless of timing.
Test type and window period matter; further testing such as an antigen/antibody assay or nucleic-acid test may be indicated under current guidance.
Symptoms establish HIV without laboratory testing.
No further action is needed unless the patient discloses a particular identity.

practiceQuestions.rationale: HIV assays have differing detection windows; nucleic-acid testing can detect infection earlier than antibody-only testing. Use current diagnostic guidance and exposure timing rather than symptoms or identity alone.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with HIV asks whether sustained viral suppression prevents sexual transmission. Which response is most consistent with CDC treatment-as-prevention information?

options.text: HIV treatment has no effect on sexual transmission.
Sustained viral suppression prevents sexual transmission of HIV; continue treatment and monitoring, and discuss other prevention needs according to the patient’s goals.
A single undetectable result means ART can be stopped.
U=U applies identically to every possible transmission route without qualification.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC supports treatment as prevention and U=U in the context of sustained viral suppression. It is not a reason to stop ART, and counseling should not overgeneralize to every route or ignore individual preference and other prevention needs.

practiceQuestions.stem: Before choosing an initial ART approach for a newly diagnosed adult, which information is most appropriate to integrate?

options.text: Only the CD4 count.
Current NIH recommendations, resistance and co-infection information, medication interactions, comorbidities, pregnancy considerations when relevant, and the patient’s preferences and access needs.
A regimen remembered from a prior year, without checking current guidance.
A regimen selected solely by a viral-load number.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ART choice is individualized and date-sensitive; NIH guidance and the complete medication/clinical context guide selection. This question intentionally does not assert a specific regimen.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient receiving ART has a rising viral load. What is the safest initial reasoning approach?

options.text: Switch immediately to a single new drug without reviewing the regimen.
Review trend and assay context, adherence and access, medication/supplement interactions, treatment and resistance history, and current guideline recommendations before decisions.
Assume nonadherence and end care.
Ignore the result if the patient feels well.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Virologic rebound has multiple possible causes. Systematic evaluation and current resistance/failure guidance are needed before regimen decisions; a single result or assumption is not enough.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which source should guide current decisions about opportunistic-infection prophylaxis in an adult with HIV?

options.text: An undated memory aid alone.
The current NIH adult/adolescent OI guideline section for the relevant pathogen, interpreted with the patient’s clinical context and medication risks.
Pediatric recommendations applied without checking population.
The viral load alone, without CD4 or pathogen context.

practiceQuestions.rationale: OI prophylaxis and treatment rules are pathogen- and context-specific and change over time. The current NIH OI guideline is the authoritative starting reference; this item avoids asserting a threshold that can change.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient requests PrEP. Which principle best supports safe, current practice?

options.text: Start without assessing HIV status because PrEP is not antiretroviral medication.
Use current CDC PrEP guidance, confirm HIV status with the recommended testing, and arrange the required ongoing follow-up for the selected prevention approach.
Require disclosure of a specific identity before discussing PrEP.
Use the same follow-up schedule for every oral and injectable option without checking the guideline.

practiceQuestions.rationale: PrEP requires HIV assessment before and during use and continuing monitoring; details depend on the product and current recommendations. Counseling should be respectful and based on clinical needs, not identity assumptions.

practiceQuestions.stem: A pregnant patient has a new HIV diagnosis. Which learning-resource navigation choice is appropriate?

options.text: Use only adult/adolescent ART guidance without checking pregnancy recommendations.
Use the current NIH perinatal HIV guideline set and coordinate prompt expert, obstetric, and pediatric/perinatal care.
Delay linkage until delivery.
Assume infant risk can be determined from one maternal screening result.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NIH maintains distinct perinatal guidance; pregnancy and infant prevention require population-specific, multidisciplinary care. The question tests source selection, not an individual treatment plan.

practiceQuestions.stem: A clinician wants to reuse a case slide from an AETC/NASC public resource in a course that will be posted online. What should they do?

options.text: Assume free viewing permits copying and public reposting.
Follow the resource’s attribution and materials-use terms; obtain permission before posting/rehosting where required, and do not copy patient records or images without verified rights.
Remove the author name and reuse the slide.
Assume public-domain status for every embedded image.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AETC/NASC guidance supports appropriately attributed use of materials unless noted, but explicitly says not to publish/post materials without creator or copyright-holder permission. Image rights and de-identification require separate care.
practiceQuestions.domain: AAHIVS IV: Professional Responsibility and Health Equity

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner asks whether completing this online course makes them eligible for an HIV board examination. Which answer is correct?

options.text: Yes; the course provides HIV board eligibility.

There is no separate ABIM HIV subspecialty board exam. ABIM offers Infectious Disease certification under its own training/eligibility rules; AAHIVM offers a separate HIV Specialist credentialing exam that is not ABMS board certification.
The AAHIVM credential is an ABMS board certification.
A one-year online course replaces an accredited fellowship.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABIM lists and sets requirements for Infectious Disease certification. AAHIVM describes its HIV Specialist as an Academy credential requiring eligibility steps and an exam. Neither this course nor institutional track listing creates eligibility.

title: Image-Guided Neurosurgery Fellowship
prerequisites: Advanced medical learner; expected completion of medical school/physician-level neurosurgical foundations or equivalent; this online course does not determine eligibility.
Prior knowledge of neuroanatomy, cross-sectional CT/MRI, neurologic examination, tumor biology, perioperative safety and evidence appraisal.
Access to a licensed clinical supervisor is required for any patient-care application; no clinical/procedural practice is authorized by this course.
objectives: Describe how clinical question, anatomy and modality selection inform image-guided neurosurgical planning.

Identify ethics, consent, privacy, licensing and research translation boundaries.

assignment.title: Image-guidance evidence-and-uncertainty case conference
assignment.prompt: For one fictional educational scenario involving a lesion near an eloquent network, prepare (1) a concise localization/differential; (2) imaging question and modality rationale; (3) a navigation/functional-imaging uncertainty map; (4) multidisciplinary tissue/management questions; (5) postoperative imaging questions; (6) a short evidence critique with citations. No real patient data or images. Do not write an operative plan or patient-specific treatment advice.

rubric.exceeds: Anatomically reasoned differential and explicit uncertainty; distinguishes finding from diagnosis.
Explains image purpose, registration/brain-shift issue and modality-specific limitations.
Uses dated authoritative sources appropriately; avoids extrapolating beyond evidence.
Escalates uncertainty to supervised multidisciplinary decision-making; no unsupervised procedure guidance.
Clear, accurate citations; uses only fictional prompt or lawful linked image resource; no PHI.

assignment.passRule: Formative only; suggested score ≥80/100 and remediation for any safety/privacy failure. Not validated against board performance.

assessment.format: Unit-level concept checks, 10 original single-best-answer questions, and evidence-and-uncertainty assignment.
assessment.interpretation: Formative self-study only; not official board questions, validated examination, certification, or guarantee of passing.

studyHours.plan: 90 hours total learner study plan (not a verified training duration): 36 hours intended specialty recordings; ~8 hours foundation recordings; 18 hours readings/evidence appraisal; 12 hours case-based reasoning; 8 hours assignments; 8 hours spaced retrieval/review. Existing verified free specialty recording time is 1.43 h, so the full target cannot be completed using current ready recordings alone. The balance requires future original films or newly verified free recordings; none are counted as ready.

mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Official programme page states the fellowship offers advanced clinical methods and translational research, fellows participate in care of patients with brain tumors and functional disorders, and curriculum spans ordering/interpretation of radiographic studies, neuro-navigation, intra-operative imaging and postoperative management. It expects original research and says an individualized clinical/research plan is developed. Eligibility statement requires completion of an ACGME-accredited programme or equivalent in home country, with possible individually considered enfolded option for senior neurosurgical residents, plus eligibility for a limited Massachusetts license. The page does not publish a detailed didactic schedule, fellowship duration, exact accreditation status or separate board exam. These remain unverified; do not infer them.

topicGaps: A current 36-hour specialty-video target remains 31.05 verified specialty hours short; the NREF additions are a dated, narrower radiosurgery supplement, not a comprehensive image-guided neurosurgery lecture series.

No detailed BWH didactic timetable, exact fellowship duration, or public full-length BWH lecture sequence is published on the official fellowship page; the training description is not a lecture ledger.

Dedicated source-led instruction remains thin in multimodal preoperative image interpretation; stereotactic coordinate and registration error budgets; functional MRI/tractography interpretation and discordance; intraoperative MRI/ultrasound workflow and brain-shift compensation; tissue sampling/pathology; postoperative imaging; and modern research evidence appraisal.

Open-access academic articles offer supporting detail but are not counted as video hours. Direct PMC access to the cited fMRI/ultrasound reviews returned anti-bot challenges during this check; the accessible Frontiers brain-shift review and 2022 ACR fMRI parameter are linked, and the blocked sources are not represented as freshly reviewed full text.

The NREF recordings are public, but most date from 2014–2015 and include disclosed industry support. Use them as historical conceptual material only; current treatment eligibility, dose, and technique require current multidisciplinary and radiation-oncology review.

The reviewed public ABNS source describes parent neurological-surgery certification; no separate image-guided neurosurgery examination was identified in the bounded sources checked on 2026-10-07. This is not proof that no credential exists elsewhere.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

boardNames: American Board of Neurological Surgery (ABNS) — neurological surgery primary certification examinations; no separate image-guided-neurosurgery board examination identified in sources reviewed.
medical.boardStatus: BWH’s public page identifies a clinical neurosurgery fellowship combining clinical methods and translational research. The ABNS public oral-exam page describes separate neurosurgery certification steps. The sources reviewed identify no separate board examination for image-guided neurosurgery; this negative claim is bounded to sources checked on 2026-10-07.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This self-study course creates no board eligibility. ABNS eligibility includes completion of a seven-year (84-month) ACGME-approved neurological surgery residency and passing the ABNS written Primary Examination for credit before the chief year, among additional requirements on its current page. Fellowship completion is not a guarantee of eligibility or certification; verify directly with ABNS.

officialProgrammes.institution: Brigham and Women’s Hospital (Harvard Medical School affiliate)
officialProgrammes.name: BWH Image Guided Fellowship / Image-guided Neurosurgery Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official programme page states the fellowship offers advanced clinical methods and translational research, fellows participate in care of patients with brain tumors and functional disorders, and curriculum spans ordering/interpretation of radiographic studies, neuro-navigation, intra-operative imaging and postoperative management. It expects original research and says an individualized clinical/research plan is developed. Eligibility statement requires completion of an ACGME-accredited programme or equivalent in home country, with possible individually considered enfolded option for senior neurosurgical residents, plus eligibility for a limited Massachusetts license. The page does not publish a detailed didactic schedule, fellowship duration, exact accreditation status or separate board exam. These remain unverified; do not infer them.

medical.programmeSourceScope: This exact institutional variant is the supplied BWH offering. No Johns Hopkins variant was assigned or discovered in the preserved item packet; do not generalize to all Harvard or Hopkins offerings. It is a named physician clinical fellowship with research component, not a generic directory label, not a research-only nonphysician supplement, and not a combined residency. Public BWH description expressly describes patient-care participation plus translational research. The public page says ACGME-approved prior training/equivalent is an entry requirement; it does not identify this fellowship itself as ACGME accredited.
sourceCaveats: Human clinical review has not been performed.
The BWH page is an institutional programme description, not proof that this specific fellowship has ACGME accreditation; it requires prior ACGME-accredited training or equivalent.
The fellowship website does not state duration, exact didactic hours, official detailed syllabus, or an image-guided fellowship board exam.
ABNS eligibility details change; recheck current board page. ABNS oral exam information includes eligibility prerequisites and case logs beyond the abbreviated course mapping.
An academic/clinical programme or residency guideline cannot establish autonomous competency, case volume, state licensure or patient outcomes.
The EANO adult diffuse glioma guideline is dated 2020; validate newer WHO/guideline updates before clinical use.
Direct PMC access to two open-access reviews was blocked by an anti-bot check; the source URLs and their indexed metadata are provided transparently.
No proprietary/login-only or shared-browser content was accessed.
Videos may be removed or restricted; recheck free public playback at course release. Durations record observed public page metadata at check date.

topicGaps: A current 36-hour specialty-video target remains 31.05 verified specialty hours short; the NREF additions are a dated, narrower radiosurgery supplement, not a comprehensive image-guided neurosurgery lecture series.

No detailed BWH didactic timetable, exact fellowship duration, or public full-length BWH lecture sequence is published on the official fellowship page; the training description is not a lecture ledger.

Dedicated source-led instruction remains thin in multimodal preoperative image interpretation; stereotactic coordinate and registration error budgets; functional MRI/tractography interpretation and discordance; intraoperative MRI/ultrasound workflow and brain-shift compensation; tissue sampling/pathology; postoperative imaging; and modern research evidence appraisal.

Open-access academic articles offer supporting detail but are not counted as video hours. Direct PMC access to the cited fMRI/ultrasound reviews returned anti-bot challenges during this check; the accessible Frontiers brain-shift review and 2022 ACR fMRI parameter are linked, and the blocked sources are not represented as freshly reviewed full text.

The NREF recordings are public, but most date from 2014–2015 and include disclosed industry support. Use them as historical conceptual material only; current treatment eligibility, dose, and technique require current multidisciplinary and radiation-oncology review.

The reviewed public ABNS source describes parent neurological-surgery certification; no separate image-guided neurosurgery examination was identified in the bounded sources checked on 2026-10-07. This is not proof that no credential exists elsewhere.
