practiceQuestions.stem: A preoperative MRI is loaded into a navigation system. After substantial tissue deformation, the displayed target still appears numerically precise. What is the central concern?

options.text: Precision of displayed coordinates guarantees anatomical accuracy.
The image-to-patient relationship may no longer represent current anatomy.
The preoperative scan becomes a histologic diagnosis.
Navigation eliminates the need for clinical examination.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A coordinate display can remain precise while registration and anatomy diverge. Brain shift is a documented limitation of preoperative-image neuronavigation; reassessment and supervised judgment matter.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult with a suspected diffuse glioma is being discussed for diagnosis. Which statement best reflects the cited EANO guidance?

options.text: Imaging alone always establishes histomolecular diagnosis.
MRI is first-choice diagnostic imaging; tissue diagnosis and molecular assessment commonly inform management.
Amino-acid PET replaces MRI and tissue diagnosis.
CSF cell-free DNA is proven screening standard for all suspected glioma.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The EANO guideline describes MRI as first-choice imaging and explains the role of tissue-based histomolecular diagnosis; it notes that liquid biopsy benefits remain to be proven in the cited guideline. Confirm any future update before clinical use.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which conclusion is safest when presurgical fMRI shows a task-related activation near a proposed lesion?

options.text: Activation guarantees that no operation can be considered.
The map is an adjunct requiring task, technical and clinical context.
The map proves the exact indispensable cortical boundary.
The result establishes patient candidacy for a particular procedure.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Presurgical fMRI has technical and clinical challenges and should be interpreted in context; it does not provide a guarantee of function or outcome.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner is asked to distinguish the BWH Image-guided Neurosurgery Fellowship from a board certification. Which is supported?

options.text: The fellowship is itself an ABNS board examination.
The public programme describes clinical and translational research fellowship training; ABNS describes separate neurosurgical certification examinations.
Completing the fellowship guarantees ABNS eligibility.
The fellowship creates a separate image-guided neurosurgery board.

practiceQuestions.rationale: BWH describes a fellowship, while ABNS outlines its primary and oral certification process. The public sources reviewed identify no separate image-guided-neurosurgery board exam; no eligibility promise should be made.

practiceQuestions.stem: What does the ACGME neurological surgery requirement of 84 months refer to?

options.text: The BWH image-guided fellowship length.
The ACGME neurological surgery residency educational programme length.
The minimum number of videos in a self-study curriculum.
The oral examination duration.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2026 ACGME requirements specify 84 months for the neurological surgery residency; this is not the duration of this fellowship or online curriculum.

practiceQuestions.stem: Why should functional imaging findings be described with uncertainty?

options.text: All imaging output is fabricated.
Technical performance, analysis and neurovascular coupling can affect functional maps.
Functional imaging is identical to pathology.
Uncertainty can be removed by adding a navigation overlay.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Presurgical fMRI has acquisition and interpretation limitations; additional displays do not erase them.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional lesion is being considered for stereotactic biopsy because open resection is not judged safely feasible. Which is the most evidence-consistent educational point?

options.text: Imaging-guided biopsy makes tissue sampling unnecessary.
Stereotactic sampling can obtain diagnostic tissue, but target/sample adequacy and clinical risks remain supervised decisions.
One sample always captures all tumor molecular heterogeneity.
A radiographic appearance substitutes for integrated diagnosis in every patient.

practiceQuestions.rationale: EANO discusses stereotactic biopsy where microsurgical resection is not safely feasible and cautions implicitly through tissue diagnosis/sampling principles that plans remain clinical decisions.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement distinguishes image-guided neurosurgery from stereotactic radiosurgery?

options.text: They are synonymous names for a single operation.
Image guidance supports intraoperative localization; radiosurgery is a radiation-based treatment concept requiring separate multidisciplinary planning.
Both guarantee complete removal of a lesion.
Radiosurgery is a type of open biopsy.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The Mount Sinai lecture treats stereotactic radiosurgery as a distinct modality and the BWH page describes image-guided operative imaging. Treatment selection is outside this course.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner wants to use an authentic MRI from TCIA in a public slide deck. What is the safest course?

options.text: Copy any image because viewing is free.
Read the specific collection/data-use conditions, maintain de-identification and citations, and avoid redistribution absent explicit rights.
Remove the title and share the DICOM anyway.
Assume all TCIA material is public domain.

practiceQuestions.rationale: TCIA offers de-identified cancer imaging, but free access is not blanket republication permission; obey collection terms and cite sources. This curriculum links to data, not copied images.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about the ABNS oral examination is accurate for the public page checked on 2026-10-07?

options.text: It is a certification exam solely in image-guided surgery.
It is a final ABNS certification step with broad clinical scenarios; published eligibility includes prior ACGME residency and primary exam prerequisites.
It is guaranteed to all fellowship graduates.
It does not test clinical judgment.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABNS describes its oral examination as a final transition to diplomate status and lists eligibility requirements, including an 84-month ACGME residency and passing the written primary examination for credit before chief year.

unitMap.text: Urologic oncology foundations, biology and evidence
coveredTopics: Urologic tumour biology, pathology and molecular testing
TNM/stage-group concepts; histology and grade; hereditary risk referral
Evidence hierarchy, trials, endpoints, bias, competing risks and patient-reported outcomes

unitMap.text: Prostate cancer detection, MRI, biopsy and risk stratification
coveredTopics: PSA screening and repeat elevation; family/genetic risk; biomarkers
Prostate MRI and PI-RADS (prostate only); biopsy strategies and pathology
Risk calculators, false negatives, overdiagnosis and shared decisions

unitMap.text: Localized and locally advanced prostate cancer
coveredTopics: Risk group and staging; organ-confined and locally advanced disease
Active surveillance versus watchful waiting; local therapy; functional outcomes
Adjuvant/salvage considerations and recurrence definitions (guideline-date checked)

unitMap.text: Advanced prostate cancer and survivorship
coveredTopics: Biochemical recurrence and staging; conventional and molecular imaging limits
Hormone-sensitive and castration-resistant disease concepts; treatment classes, not prescribing
Germline/somatic testing, family implications, toxicity monitoring and survivorship

unitMap.text: Non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer
coveredTopics: Hematuria work-up, cystoscopy, TURBT and upper-tract evaluation
Grade/stage/risk groups, CIS, variant histology and re-resection logic
Intravesical therapy, surveillance, BCG shortage/shortage-era alternatives and salvage pathways

unitMap.text: Muscle-invasive bladder and upper-tract urothelial carcinoma
coveredTopics: MIBC staging, perioperative systemic therapy, cystectomy/diversion and trimodality therapy
Upper tract evaluation, risk stratification, ureteroscopy/pathology and kidney-sparing approaches
Renal function, frailty, shared decisions and follow-up

unitMap.text: Localized renal cell carcinoma and renal masses
coveredTopics: RCC histology, imaging phases, staging and renal function
Small renal mass decision making and nephron-sparing principles
Renal vein/IVC tumour thrombus, adrenal/nodal evaluation and hereditary syndromes

unitMap.text: Advanced RCC, systemic therapy and perioperative care
coveredTopics: Risk models and histologic subtype; systemic therapy classes and combinations
Surgery/systemic therapy sequencing and selective cytoreductive surgery
Response assessment, treatment toxicity, palliative care and clinical trials

unitMap.text: Testicular germ-cell tumours
coveredTopics: Ultrasound, markers before/after orchiectomy, histology and staging
Risk-adapted stage I management and post-chemotherapy residual mass reasoning
Fertility preservation, late effects and survivorship

unitMap.text: Penile, urethral, adrenal and uncommon GU tumours
coveredTopics: Penile primary staging, inguinal nodes and morbidity of nodal procedures
Primary urethral cancer, adrenal cortical cancer, sarcoma and rare entities
Genitourinary pathology review, referral and uncertainty

unitMap.text: Complex oncologic surgery, reconstruction, complications and ethics
coveredTopics: Open, laparoscopic and robotic approaches; lymph-node templates; margins
Urinary diversion, reconstruction, perioperative complications and salvage pathways
Informed consent, equity, referral and no-procedure authorization

unitMap.text: Research methods, clinical trials, quality, equity and career scholarship
coveredTopics: Research design and ethics; registry/data privacy; biostatistics
Clinical trials and evidence communication; health services/lab research boundaries
Quality improvement, equity, shared decisions and academic scholarship

topicGaps: Observed unique, free, topic-relevant recordings total 12.789444 hours, leaving 23.210556 hours below the 36-hour floor; authored episodes are scripts, not recorded/runtime-verified hours.

Added free recordings broaden coverage in MIBC multidisciplinary care, penile malignancy and bladder-cancer trial updates. UTUC appears in a relevant JHU recording whose exact runtime was not verifiable, so it remains excluded from the counted ledger.

No adequately verified dedicated long-form recordings were located for GU pathology, hereditary counseling, rare urethral/adrenal/sarcoma entities, complex reconstruction/diversion, operative complications, or comprehensive survivorship; planned/source-based teaching does not erase these source gaps.

Even where recordings exist, the public selection is not the SUO core curriculum and does not replace clinical training. Rapidly changing systemic therapy, imaging, guideline editions, molecular testing, and eligibility must be rechecked in current primary guidance.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.boardStatus: Urologic oncology is a physician subspecialty fellowship within urology. ABU general urology certification includes oncology among its domains; ABU homepage lists subspecialty certifications in Pediatric Urology and Urogynecology and Reconstructive Pelvic Surgery, not Urologic Oncology. No separate ABU urologic-oncology board exam was found. SUO accredits its own 2-year fellowship programmes and requires fellows to take OKAT each fellowship year; SUO fellowship/OKAT status is not ABU board certification. The historical SUO discussion of a possible focused practice designation is not proof of a currently available personal certification; verify with ABU/SUO directly.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent course does not confer ABU eligibility, SUO fellowship completion/accreditation, OKAT credit, Focused Practice Designation, licensure, or board status. medical.programmeSourceScope: The user packet supplies the MGB/Harvard fellowship. Official SUO-approved-program evidence additionally identifies Johns Hopkins, so that distinct exact institutional variant is preserved here. This is a self-study course mapped to the common SUO urologic-oncology domains, not a representation of either institution’s internal didactic curriculum, rotations, eligibility, case volume or assessment. MGB webpage lists multidisciplinary rotations but no block schedule. SUO requirements specify minimum structure for SUO-accredited programmes; not a claim that any named fellow performed the guideline examples of case volumes.
sourceCaveats: MGB page and Johns Hopkins official page were fetched. MGB says the programme is now the Combined Harvard Urologic Oncology Fellowship. SUO lists exact name “Combined Harvard Medical School Urologic Oncology Fellowship Program” and separately lists “Johns Hopkins”; JHU programme page identifies its distinct two-year clinical/research fellowship. Preserve variants rather than merging the institutions.

SUO accreditation is not ACGME accreditation; ACGME urology requirements are for the prerequisite residency. The SUO requirements’ typical index-case figures are general guidance and are not attributed to any specific fellow or named institution.

No separate ABU urologic oncology board examination was found: ABU lists only Pediatric Urology and URPS as subspecialty certifications and its general urology examination includes oncology. SUO OKAT is a secure annual knowledge assessment and SUO fellowship requirement, not a separate board. SUO historical page says separate ABU certification did not proceed. 2018 FPD discussion is historical and not current confirmation.

MGB page gives high-level rotations and research career aims but no granular rotation calendar, exact didactic set or public case-volume data. Johns Hopkins page gives two-year clinical/research structure, not its exact current schedule/case counts. No private or login-only programme content accessed.

Clinical references checked on 2026-10-07. NCI PDQs last shown updates: prostate May 14, 2025; kidney May 13, 2025; testis May 16, 2025; penile May 7, 2025; adrenal December 13, 2024. Re-check living guidelines and drug indications before teaching or clinical use.
ABU subspecialty detail page returned 403 on stateless fetch; ABU homepage clearly lists its current subspecialty certifications. No login or browser bypass attempted.

Video runtimes were directly observed from public YouTube watch page player displays and/or clearly rendered runtime listing during page fetch on the check date. Stream availability is volatile; this ledger is not a guarantee of future playback. Public free viewing is not reuse permission. Only ten unique canonical YouTube IDs are counted.

Human clinical review was not performed. This course is independent and has no Harvard/JHU/MGB affiliation, no accredited training, no clinical supervision, no licensure, no board eligibility, no certification and no guarantee of passing or competence.

topicGaps: Observed unique, free, topic-relevant recordings total 12.789444 hours, leaving 23.210556 hours below the 36-hour floor; authored episodes are scripts, not recorded/runtime-verified hours.

Added free recordings broaden coverage in MIBC multidisciplinary care, penile malignancy and bladder-cancer trial updates. UTUC appears in a relevant JHU recording whose exact runtime was not verifiable, so it remains excluded from the counted ledger.

No adequately verified dedicated long-form recordings were located for GU pathology, hereditary counseling, rare urethral/adrenal/sarcoma entities, complex reconstruction/diversion, operative complications, or comprehensive survivorship; planned/source-based teaching does not erase these source gaps.

Even where recordings exist, the public selection is not the SUO core curriculum and does not replace clinical training. Rapidly changing systemic therapy, imaging, guideline editions, molecular testing, and eligibility must be rechecked in current primary guidance.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which action is most appropriate after one newly elevated PSA in an otherwise stable, asymptomatic person before ordering MRI or biopsy?

options.text: Proceed directly to systematic biopsy
Repeat PSA after an interval appropriate to transient causes and clinical context
Give empiric antibiotics despite no infection
Use PSA velocity alone to decide

practiceQuestions.rationale: AUA/SUO guideline statement recommends repeating a newly elevated PSA before secondary biomarkers, imaging or biopsy. Evaluate infection, instrumentation and retention context; empiric antibiotics are not recommended for an asymptomatic elevation.

practiceQuestions.stem: An elevated PSA is repeated and normalizes. Which statement best reflects decision reasoning?

options.text: Cancer is definitively excluded
Further assessment depends on overall risk and context; normalization can avoid reflex work-up
Biopsy is mandatory because the first result was high
PSA velocity alone resolves uncertainty

practiceQuestions.rationale: AUA notes a substantial proportion normalize at repeat. A normalized value does not rule out all malignancy; integrate risk, patient preferences and guideline pathways.

practiceQuestions.stem: A bladder TURBT report says high-grade T1 urothelial carcinoma and muscularis propria is absent. Which issue is most important to resolve?

options.text: No issue if imaging is normal
Staging adequacy and need for repeat evaluation/resection per current guideline
Assign a PI-RADS score
Assume muscle-invasive disease is excluded

practiceQuestions.rationale: Muscle presence is central to assessing invasion; guidelines support careful staging and repeat resection in indicated high-risk/understaged settings. PI-RADS applies to prostate MRI.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about muscle-invasive bladder cancer is most accurate?

options.text: There is only one universally appropriate curative pathway
Cisplatin-based perioperative systemic treatment plus cystectomy is an important pathway; chemoradiation-based bladder preservation is another selected multidisciplinary option
Radiation is never used
No upper-tract imaging is needed

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCI PDQ describes cystectomy after cisplatin-based neoadjuvant therapy and chemoradiation as major curative-intent approaches; selection depends on patient and tumour factors and current evidence.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 3 cm enhancing renal mass is found incidentally. What is the best initial educational framing?

options.text: All such lesions require immediate radical nephrectomy
Consider imaging characterization, renal function, patient factors, possible biopsy and active surveillance/nephron-sparing options under current guidance
Use LI-RADS
Assume benign because under 4 cm

practiceQuestions.rationale: RCC work-up and management are individualized. AUA/EAU/NCI sources cover assessment, function and management options; no size-only rule diagnoses benignity.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which renal cancer statement is correct?

options.text: Renal vein/IVC tumour extension is irrelevant to stage
Renal mass decisions must consider anatomy, renal reserve, tumour features and patient context
All nodal dissection improves survival
Tumour thrombus automatically means distant metastasis

practiceQuestions.rationale: RCC staging includes extent into veins and perinephric structures; renal function and anatomy inform care. Do not extrapolate a single factor into an absolute decision.

practiceQuestions.stem: For a testicular germ-cell tumour, which marker set is standard in staging/risk discussions?

options.text: PSA, CEA and CA19-9
AFP, beta-hCG and LDH
CA-125, HE4 and LDH
Troponin and BNP

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCI PDQ describes AFP, beta-hCG and LDH as relevant serum tumour markers; interpret with histology, timing and staging.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is the best response to a question about risk-adapted stage I testicular cancer management?

options.text: All patients must receive chemotherapy
Orchiectomy is followed by evidence-based discussion of surveillance and other options according to histology, risk, ability to follow up and preferences
RPLND is mandatory for every seminoma
No long-term survivorship counselling is needed

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCI PDQ outlines distinct stage- and histology-dependent options. Avoid blanket treatment recommendations; fertility and late effects matter.

practiceQuestions.stem: In penile squamous-cell cancer, what is the key exam distinction about nodal assessment?

options.text: Only distant PET defines all stage
Inguinal nodal status is clinically important and must be considered with primary tumour stage and pathology
PI-RADS defines primary lesion risk
A palpable groin node proves metastasis without differential

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCI PDQ TNM includes inguinal/pelvic nodes; inflammatory causes can mimic nodal disease. Assessment and management are specialist-led.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes credentials?

options.text: SUO OKAT is the ABU’s separate Urologic Oncology board exam
ABU general Urology certification includes oncology; ABU lists Pediatric Urology and URPS subspecialty certifications, while SUO fellowships/OKAT are separate
ACGME accredits SUO oncology fellowships
Completing this online course grants ABU eligibility

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABU public homepage and initial-certification page distinguish its general certification and listed subspecialty certifications. SUO programme requirements state SUO, not ACGME, accredits its oncology fellowships; OKAT is an annual fellow assessment.

title: Pituitary Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (institutional surgical subspecialty offering; not an independent board specialty)-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Advanced physician learner with completed neurological surgery residency (or equivalent home-country programme) expected by MGB; official page also requires a valid Massachusetts medical license. This independent course is appropriate only as supplementary study for clinicians/trainees with anatomy, neurobiology, endocrinology and MRI fundamentals; it does not confer admission, licensure or procedural readiness.
objectives: Integrate sellar anatomy, imaging, endocrine physiology and neuro-ophthalmic risk in educational cases.
Evaluate common pituitary disorders and formulate evidence-aware differential/management questions for a multidisciplinary team.
Describe endoscopic endonasal surgical workflow conceptually and identify safety boundaries without claiming procedural competency.
Appraise pituitary evidence and communicate uncertainty, follow-up and escalation needs.

units.title: Foundations: sellar anatomy, physiology, and team-based care
objectives: Map anterior/posterior pituitary, stalk, optic apparatus, cavernous sinus, ICA, sphenoid and skull-base relationships.
Explain hypothalamic-pituitary axes and feedback at a level useful for case interpretation.
Assign endocrine, neurosurgical, ENT, ophthalmic, radiology, pathology and radiation-oncology roles.
topics: Anatomy; normal hormonal axes; PitNET nomenclature; multidisciplinary conference
Board: ABNS tumor/sellar and general clinical reasoning (not a separate pituitary exam).
boardDomains: ABNS primary neurological surgery: tumor/sellar reasoning where relevant; ABNS exam is broad and not pituitary-fellowship certification.
units.casePractice: Use the linked open case/data resource only under its terms; no patient records or images copied. Work through a fictional case vignette and state uncertainty.
units.assessment: Short-answer anatomy/reporting or differential task; graded with rubric: factual accuracy 40%, differential/uncertainty 25%, safety/escalation 25%, source citation 10%.

units.title: Sellar imaging, reporting, and differential diagnosis
objectives: Select a dedicated pituitary MRI protocol and identify key structures without overcalling subtle enhancement.

medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional 48-year-old has a sellar lesion incidentally found on non-pituitary brain MRI. Which broad next-step framework best matches current consensus?

options.text: Declare a nonfunctioning adenoma based on incidental discovery.
Arrange dedicated imaging if existing images are insufficient, initial endocrine testing, clinical assessment and vision evaluation as indicated.
Skip hormone testing if the lesion is small.
Proceed directly to transsphenoidal surgery.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2025 consensus recommends pituitary hormone testing at initial presentation regardless of size and dedicated pituitary MRI in most cases when existing imaging is insufficient; clinical/visual context guides referrals.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which situation most clearly calls for formal visual-field assessment?

options.text: Any lesion under 10 mm.
A lesion abutting or compressing the optic nerves/chiasm.
An isolated mildly elevated prolactin result.
Normal dedicated MRI.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Visual-field testing is indicated when the lesion abuts or compresses the optic apparatus or symptoms suggest visual compromise; assess in clinical context.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional person with known sellar mass presents with sudden severe headache and acute visual deterioration. What is the best educational response?

options.text: Schedule routine follow-up MRI in a year.
Urgent clinical assessment for a possible sellar emergency including apoplexy.
Start self-directed hormone therapy.
Assume migraine because headache is common.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Acute severe headache and visual change can indicate apoplexy or other emergency; immediate clinician-led evaluation is needed. No self-treatment advice is supplied.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about small sellar MRI abnormalities is most accurate?

options.text: Dynamic enhancement alone proves microadenoma.
Artifact and normal gland enhancement can mimic small lesions; use dedicated protocol and interpret cautiously.
Every lesion is best classified by CT alone.
A single sequence establishes hormone function.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Dynamic MRI may help localization, but artifacts and normal enhancement can create false positives; biochemical function is not established by imaging.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which biochemical marker is central to screening for GH excess in a pituitary lesion?

options.text: Serum IGF-1.
Serum sodium alone.
Random ACTH alone.
Urinary prolactin.

practiceQuestions.rationale: IGF-1 is a key screening biomarker for acromegaly; confirmatory evaluation depends on assay/context and current consensus.

practiceQuestions.stem: According to the 2023 prolactinoma consensus, which agent is generally preferred when dopamine-agonist treatment is selected?

options.text: Cabergoline.
Hydrocortisone.
Desmopressin.
Octreotide in every patient.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Cabergoline is the preferred dopamine agonist for many prolactinomas because of efficacy and tolerability; surgery and other options require individualized multidisciplinary decisions.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which choice describes MGB Pituitary Fellowship accurately?

options.text: An endocrinology residency with an endocrinology board examination.
A one-year endoscopic pituitary/skull-base surgical fellowship including clinical/lab research and dissection-lab experience.
A pituitary-specific ABNS board certification.
A public online course conferring licensure.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Official MGB page states one-year design, clinical and laboratory research, endoscopic techniques and dissection-lab training; its stated prerequisites include prior accredited residency or equivalent and Massachusetts license.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is an accurate ABNS exam distinction?

options.text: Completing a pituitary fellowship alone grants ABNS certification.
ABNS primary certification requires a specified seven-year ACGME neurosurgery residency pathway and written/oral requirements; no separate pituitary exam is described on the cited page.
ACGME certifies all pituitary fellows directly.
The ABNS oral exam covers only pituitary tumors.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABNS describes a broad primary pathway including seven-year residency, written exam and oral examination; the fellowship is not a substitute for requirements.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional lesion contacts the chiasm but has no reported hormone excess. Which inference is best?

options.text: The contact automatically mandates surgery.
The anatomy is a reason for timely specialist and visual assessment, but management requires individualized clinical integration.
Observation is always correct.
A normal hormone panel eliminates visual risk.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Chiasmal proximity prompts specialist discussion and visual assessment; the consensus calls for individualized decisions, not automatic surgery.

practiceQuestions.stem: A research MRI dataset is used for a class exercise. Which practice is appropriate?

options.text: Attempt to identify participants using dates and facial features.
Rehost images without reviewing license.
Use the dataset under its stated terms, do not attempt re-identification, and distinguish research images from a clinical reference standard.
Treat model segmentation as ground truth.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The OpenNeuro set is de-identified research data with stated terms and license conditions; the page requires no re-identification and careful attribution; its benchmark masks do not establish clinical truth for any patient.

title: Skull Base Fellowship
prerequisites: Intended learner: neurosurgery resident at senior level or post-residency neurosurgeon, or another clinician with advanced neuroanatomy and supervised skull-base exposure. This is a pedagogical level, not a programme admission rule.

Prerequisite understanding: cranial neuroanatomy, neurosurgical imaging, tumor and vascular basics, neuroendocrine/cranial-nerve assessment, evidence appraisal and professional privacy/consent duties.

Online study cannot substitute for cadaveric anatomy lab, operating-room observation, supervised procedural performance, case logs or local credentialing. No unsupervised practice or patient-care decision is authorized.
objectives: Explain actual MGB/CAST/NASBS track distinctions and the ABNS general-board boundary.
Organize skull-base anatomy by compartment, foramina, critical cranial nerves, vascular/venous relationships and craniocervical transitions.
Use clinical presentation, neuro-ophthalmic/audiovestibular/endocrine assessment and imaging to construct a differential while stating uncertainty.
Compare conceptual open, endoscopic endonasal, lateral, posterior and far-lateral route families without asserting a universal preferred approach.
Appraise common and selected rare skull-base disease domains, multidisciplinary options, complications, follow-up and research evidence limits.
Interpret CAST’s current programme and case-log rules without equating institutional case counts with an individual’s competence.
Use public authentic case resources lawfully: link only, do not rehost, and do not assume consent/de-identification beyond verified statements.

topicGaps: Observed free public recording ledger now totals 14.0975 hours across 24 unique videos, including 2 newly appended recordings and 1 previously listed ACNS recording reclassified after duration verification. The 36-hour floor remains unmet by 21.9025 hours; no script, plan, source reading, or supervised clinical activity is counted as rendered video.

The added EANS/ACNS material improves parasellar/cavernous-sinus, lab-to-OR anatomy, approach-comparison, and complication discussion, but overall viewing remains weighted toward anatomy, approaches, and selected cases.

Diagnostic evaluation, pathology-specific treatment evidence, vascular/congenital/infectious lesions, reconstruction/CSF-leak pathways, longitudinal outcomes, research methods, and multidisciplinary decision-making still require broader current primary literature and faculty-supervised teaching; public talks do not supply a complete curriculum.

An explicit complete MGB didactic syllabus/rotation sequence and programme-specific case outcomes remain unavailable in reviewed public sources. No dedicated ABNS Skull Base examination or fellowship-specific board blueprint was identified; the course maps only to public parent-specialty domains.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

boardNames: American Board of Neurological Surgery (ABNS) — general neurological surgery certification; skull-base topics appear within ABNS general/Tumor oral-exam scope, but no separate ABNS Skull Base board examination/certificate was found.
medical.boardStatus: As checked 2026-10-07: CAST publishes skull-base fellowship programme requirements and lists Mass General Brigham among CAST-accredited programme entries. ABNS describes one general neurological-surgery certification pathway and an oral Tumor focus that includes skull-base tumors/endoscopic surgery. It does not publish a separate Skull Base board exam or individual skull-base certificate. NASBS match is administrative selection, distinct from both. No fellowship-specific ABNS exam blueprint or exam weighting was located; course alignment is only to public CAST education requirements and ABNS broad domains, not a formal blueprint.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: MGB states candidates must have completed or be in their senior year of an ACGME-accredited programme or equivalent in their home country; CAST standards for a CAST-accredited post-residency fellowship require satisfactory completion of an ACGME or foreign-equivalent accredited neurological-surgery residency. A NASBS-listed BWH programme has distinct published match fields and eligibility details; verify directly with each programme. ABNS board eligibility depends on ABNS requirements and the individual’s training/certification trajectory, not on this fellowship or course. Current rules can change. Independent self-study grants no board eligibility, exam credit, licence, fellowship appointment or operative competence.

officialProgrammes.name: Skull Base and Microneurosurgery Fellowship (official page breadcrumb/title is Skull Base Fellowship)
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page places it under Fellowship / Neurosurgery. MGB says it began in 2010; describes complex skull-base pathology and microneurosurgery, technical/clinical supervision, open and endoscopic approaches, lab-based anatomy refinement, operative decision/planning/perioperative care and scholarship. Candidates have completed or are in senior year of ACGME-accredited or equivalent programme, plus recommendation/scholarship; fellowship completion certificate. Page does not publish a complete schedule, rotations, exact duration, case counts, individual case logs or board eligibility. CAST’s current list separately lists Mass General Brigham with Linda Bi as director; the MGB overview itself does not explicitly state accreditation.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The syllabus uses the MGB Skull Base and Microneurosurgery clinical fellowship as the target track, while preserving exact related institutional evidence. CAST lists a Mass General Brigham Skull Base programme, director Linda Bi. NASBS’s 2026 match entry separately names Brigham and Women’s Endoscopic Pituitary and Skull Base Fellowship, director Timothy R. Smith, duration one year and CAST Accredited: No. Do not collapse the two programme records into one: official page names, directors and CAST statuses diverge, and the reviewed sources do not resolve their relationship. The MGB page does not provide a public detailed rotation schedule or case log. The CAST 2026 framework sets broad programme standards; it is not proof of this individual fellow’s case volume. No research-only or nonphysician track is included.
sourceCaveats: MGB’s official programme page is current for public offering scope but does not publish complete rotations, case volumes, accreditation statement or board credential outcomes.

CAST’s April 2026 requirements are general standards; programme accreditation list and match directory are distinct evidence sources. MGB page/CAST/NASBS records have programme name/director/status differences; affiliation between similarly situated offerings is unresolved.

ABNS pages concern general neurological surgery board requirements. No independent skull-base board certificate/exam found in pages reviewed; absence-of-evidence is not a guarantee that no other credential exists.

A CNS guideline URL extraction returned an unrelated pediatric-hydrocephalus page despite correct vestibular-schwannoma URL. It is flagged for revalidation and no recommendations were used to justify clinical answers.
Clinical guidelines and surgical techniques evolve. Clinical decision claims require updated source review and human specialist review.

Patient videos are authentic public-host footage, but consent/de-identification and license for derivative educational use could not be independently verified. Link-only; no patient imagery or records copied.
No human clinical review has been performed. No simulated patient case represents a real person.

title: Clinical Nutrition Support Fellowship

prerequisites: MD/DO and completion of categorical residency or equivalent advanced physician learner background; BWH published entry language is completed medical residency or at least three years of general surgery residency.

objectives: Synthesize nutrition status from history, examination, intake trajectory, anthropometry, function and laboratory context without overinterpreting inflammatory markers.

topicGaps: Observed free recordings now total 5.548056 h of the 36 h target; 30.451944 h remain. TargetMinutes in the originalClipPlan are production planning only and are never counted as recorded or verified hours.

Existing ready media still disproportionately covers adult ICU/EN/PN and home nutrition. New pediatric enteral recording adds 59:32 but is commercial-publisher symposium content; no new verified recording fills broad core physiology, obesity/metabolic disease, renal/cardiac/pulmonary/hepatic/oncology, pediatric/neonatal PN, ethics or evidence appraisal end-to-end.

The board blueprint spans general nutrition (35%), assessment (10%), obesity/metabolic (20%), disease-specific nutrition (25%) and nutrition support (10%). Public recordings found here do not cover those proportions comprehensively; authored scripts are teaching supplements and remain unrecorded.

Pediatric domains have some short/limited recording coverage, but no verified, comprehensive and independent neonatal/pediatric lecture set was established. The source-publisher page for ASPEN Nutrition Support Fundamentals says its recordings are available for purchase/through its eLearning Center; they are not free public media and were excluded.

The additional plans identify a plausible, non-overlapping source-based production queue for the residual 30.451944 h. They do not show 36 h feasibility as existing public free recordings, and there is no assurance all planned clips can be produced to that length without oversimplification or repetition.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.trackType: Clinical physician fellowship (post-residency, one-year; institutional programme listing, not a categorical residency)
boardNames: National Board of Physician Nutrition Specialists (NBPNS) — Certification Examination for Physician Nutrition Specialists®

National Board for Nutrition Support Certification (NBNSC) — Certified Nutrition Support Clinician® (CNSC®) examination (multidisciplinary; BWH page says fellow is expected to sit the ASPEN examination)
Board of Pharmacy Specialties (BPS) — Board Certified Nutrition Support Pharmacist (BCNSP), pharmacist-only supplementary credential
medical.boardStatus: Nutrition support fellowship is a clinical training track, not itself a standalone ABMS-recognized physician specialty/subspecialty. NBPNS offers a separate physician certification examination (physician nutrition specialist); CNSC is a separate multidisciplinary credential. BWH’s public page expects the fellow to sit the ASPEN CNSC exam. The public ABMS member-board roster does not list clinical nutrition as an ABMS specialty/subspecialty; this does not negate NBPNS’s independent credential. No claim of a separate ABMS nutrition-support board exam is made.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent course confers no credential and creates no eligibility. NBPNS’s current public exam page requires an active medical license, active ABMS/osteopathic/equivalent primary specialty certification, at least two of its listed nutrition expertise criteria, application/fee and board approval; criteria are reviewed annually. The BWH programme describes post-residency/prior surgical residency eligibility. CNSC and NBPNS are not interchangeable. Verify current rules directly with the boards.

officialProgrammes.name: BWH Nutrition Support Service Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page describes a one-year physician clinical fellowship after completed medical residency or at least three years of general surgery residency; GI, critical care, primary care and anesthesia-with-critical-care-focus candidates are encouraged. It lists enteral/parenteral support and settings spanning medical/surgical ICU, burn/trauma, cardiothoracic ICU, NICU, transplant and ambulatory practice (~30 outpatients), plus CSPH research collaboration. It expects the fellow to sit the ASPEN CNSC exam. No public rotation calendar, lecture recordings, hours, patient-volume ledger, ACGME accreditation determination, or guarantee of certification was found; do not infer them.

medical.programmeSourceScope: One exact institutional variant preserved from input packet: Brigham and Women’s Hospital, BWH Nutrition Support Service Fellowship. The official page calls it a clinical physician fellowship and an MGB graduate-medical-education fellowship tagged Surgery; it is neither a combined residency nor a research-only postdoc or generic directory heading. NBPNS also lists it in a survey-derived physician nutrition fellowship directory, but that listing is not accreditation evidence. The course is not affiliated with Harvard, Johns Hopkins, BWH, MGB, ASPEN, ACGME, ABMS or NBPNS.
sourceCaveats: BWH public official page supports the programme classification and published clinical scope; it does not expose actual internal lecture materials, service/rotation hours or clinical volume. Do not infer accreditation, examination outcome, curriculum equivalency or guarantees.

Current credentials are distinct: BWH says the fellow is expected to sit CNSC. NBPNS separately offers physician PNS certification. ASPEN lists BPS pharmacy nutrition support as a distinct pharmacist credential. Confirm annual rules directly.

ABMS roster consulted on 2026-10-07; no nutrition specialty/subspecialty is listed there. NBPNS is a separate credentialing body. ACGME Common Program Requirements explain accredited GME generally, not this programme’s accreditation.

ACGME November 2025 task force announcement is an initiative, not evidence that this independent course or the fellowship holds ACGME recognition. Public April 2026 specialty-nutrition requirement draft proposes a July 1, 2027 effective date; it was not binding on the date checked.

Only six unique public-video IDs with observed player durations are counted. One additional ESPEN video has unknown duration and is excluded. Free viewing is not a license to download, mirror or rehost. Public watch-page availability can change.

ASPEN 2026 video discloses sponsor support; Oley recordings disclose commercial support. Oley itself says videos/conference presentations are not clinically reviewed. Use current independent guidance to resolve claims.
ESPEN ICU guideline is 2023 and population-specific; NICE CG32 last updated 2017; use current guidance and local protocol. Historical lectures are not authoritative standards.

No patient images, records, protected board questions, proprietary course content or screenshots were copied. The linked clinical case report is an author-published case with IRB approval noted; no case facts/images are reproduced. Clinical actions require licensed, supervised clinicians and current institutional policies.

Human clinical review is NOT PERFORMED. This is independent education and grants no affiliation, accredited training, licensure, eligibility, procedure competence, certification or guaranteed board result.

topicGaps: Observed free recordings now total 5.548056 h of the 36 h target; 30.451944 h remain. TargetMinutes in the originalClipPlan are production planning only and are never counted as recorded or verified hours.

Existing ready media still disproportionately covers adult ICU/EN/PN and home nutrition. New pediatric enteral recording adds 59:32 but is commercial-publisher symposium content; no new verified recording fills broad core physiology, obesity/metabolic disease, renal/cardiac/pulmonary/hepatic/oncology, pediatric/neonatal PN, ethics or evidence appraisal end-to-end.

The board blueprint spans general nutrition (35%), assessment (10%), obesity/metabolic (20%), disease-specific nutrition (25%) and nutrition support (10%). Public recordings found here do not cover those proportions comprehensively; authored scripts are teaching supplements and remain unrecorded.

Pediatric domains have some short/limited recording coverage, but no verified, comprehensive and independent neonatal/pediatric lecture set was established. The source-publisher page for ASPEN Nutrition Support Fundamentals says its recordings are available for purchase/through its eLearning Center; they are not free public media and were excluded.

The additional plans identify a plausible, non-overlapping source-based production queue for the residual 30.451944 h. They do not show 36 h feasibility as existing public free recordings, and there is no assurance all planned clips can be produced to that length without oversimplification or repetition.

practiceQuestions.stem: A hospitalized adult with a functioning gastrointestinal tract cannot meet nutritional needs orally. Which general route principle is best supported?

options.text: Use PN routinely because it preserves gut function best.
Consider enteral nutrition when oral intake is inadequate and the GI tract is functional, while individualizing for contraindications and tolerance.
Choose jejunal access because it eliminates aspiration risk.
Route choice is determined only by anticipated duration.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Enteral nutrition is generally considered when the gut functions but oral intake is inadequate. The exact access and route depend on clinical context; jejunal feeding does not eliminate aspiration risk.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional ICU case has persistent inadequate EN delivery despite a functioning gut. Which approach to supplemental PN is most defensible for a board-style discussion?

options.text: Initiate PN automatically on ICU admission for every patient.
Discuss risk, prior intake, expected duration, illness phase, delivery gap and guideline evidence with the nutrition team; avoid a universal start-time claim.
Avoid PN under all circumstances when a gut is present.
Add PN solely because albumin is low.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Supplemental PN is a patient- and context-dependent strategy. Albumin is influenced by inflammation and is not a standalone nutrition diagnosis; early routine supplementation is not a universal default.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with prolonged negligible intake begins calorie reintroduction. Which laboratory pattern warrants particular concern for refeeding-related change?

options.text: A falling phosphate, potassium and/or magnesium trend during the first several days.
A single low albumin value without context.
A rise in HDL alone.
A normal serum sodium alone.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASPEN consensus defines refeeding severity through declines in phosphorus, potassium and/or magnesium within five days of calorie reintroduction, with organ dysfunction/thiamine-related manifestations in severe cases. Evaluate other causes and the full context.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best describes the published BWH Nutrition Support Service Fellowship?

options.text: A four-year categorical residency for all trainees.

A one-year physician clinical fellowship after medical residency or at least three years of general surgery residency; published exposures include ICU, burn/trauma, NICU, transplant and ambulatory service.
A nonclinical research postdoc for dietitians only.
A credential that itself confers state licensure.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official MGB programme page states a one-year clinical physician fellowship, eligibility, clinical settings and expected CNSC exam sitting; it does not grant licensure or replace prior residency.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner has completed this independent course. Which conclusion about physician certification eligibility is correct?

options.text: They are automatically eligible for the NBPNS exam.
Course completion grants CNSC and NBPNS diplomate status.
The course grants no credential; NBPNS has separate published medical-license, primary-board-certification and expertise criteria with board review.
The course is an ACGME-accredited fellowship.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NBPNS eligibility requires active physician licensure and primary specialty certification plus at least two specified nutrition-expertise criteria and board approval. Independent self-study is not a recognized substitute.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately distinguishes CNSC from physician nutrition specialist certification?

options.text: CNSC is a multidisciplinary nutrition support certification offered through NBNSC; NBPNS operates a separate physician-specific certification examination.
CNSC is an ABMS subspecialty limited to surgeons.
NBPNS and CNSC are identical examinations.
Neither requires an examination.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASPEN describes CNSC as a multidisciplinary credential for physicians, dietitians, nurses, pharmacists and physician assistants; NBPNS separately offers a physician certification examination.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is the best description of the NBPNS examination content blueprint?

options.text: Only PN prescribing and line procedures.
General nutrition 35%, status assessment 10%, obesity/metabolic conditions 20%, disease-specific nutrition 25%, EN/PN support 10%.
Only general medicine domains.
The blueprint is unpublished.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The current NBPNS exam summary lists those five weighted domains; this course maps units to them but is not official exam content.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which conclusion is justified by the official BWH programme page?

options.text: It publishes a fully itemized protected lecture curriculum and exact clinical case counts.
It describes clinical training scope and settings but does not publish rotation hours, a public lecture ledger, or patient volume totals.
It promises board passage.
All listed rotations are separately ACGME-accredited fellowships.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official page outlines programme duration, broad competencies and settings but provides no rotation hours or patient volume data. Do not infer undocumented counts or guarantees.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner wishes to reuse a clinical image from a public patient story or case article in a slide. Which policy is correct?

options.text: Free viewing automatically gives rehosting rights.
Do not copy or rehost any patient image/record; use a link or only explicitly licensed/de-identified material within its specific terms and permissions.
Remove the name and use the image.
Reproduce screenshots for educational use without checking terms.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Public access does not imply a reuse license. Patient records and clinical images are not bundled with this course; any reuse requires explicit rights and appropriate de-identification.

practiceQuestions.stem: Why should a guideline reading assignment identify the publication date and limitations?

options.text: Guidelines never change.
Nutrition recommendations depend on population, methods, evidence certainty and update date; a current professional decision needs the applicable up-to-date primary source.
Dates matter only for board examination scheduling.
A single public lecture overrides formal guidelines.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The course includes dated guideline resources and older materials. Appraise their applicability and date; use current local policy and qualified clinical review for actual care.

title: Brain Injury Medicine Fellowship
prerequisites: Graduate physician learners with prior medical degree; the official ACGME fellowship is post-residency advanced training.

For accredited BIM fellowship entry, 2026 ACGME requirements specify a qualifying residency in child neurology, neurology, physical medicine and rehabilitation, psychiatry, or sports medicine, subject to stated exceptional-applicant provisions. This course itself does not evaluate credentials.
Baseline neuroanatomy, neurologic examination, clinical epidemiology, evidence appraisal and foundational rehabilitation concepts.
Intended for board-level physician self-study; not for independent treatment or procedural practice.
objectives: Map traumatic and nontraumatic brain injury etiologies to neurologic, cognitive/behavioral, psychiatric, pain/sleep, systemic and functional sequelae.
Use the 2026 ABPMR blueprint to organize broad clinical reasoning across its six weighted domains.
Build safe differential, escalation, evaluation, functional assessment, goal setting and care-transition reasoning from authoritative sources.
Compare population- and time-specific mTBI guidance without applying a guideline outside its stated scope.
Interpret the limits of published evidence, fictional cases, public videos, examination practice and self-study.

units.casePractice: Construct a transfer checklist for a hypothetical stable/unstable referral.
units.assessment: Rubric: safety escalation, medication/complication continuity, goals, records, caregiver context.

assignment.title: Longitudinal fictional-case rehabilitation synthesis
assignment.instructions: Using one explicitly fictional case scenario supplied in course exercises, create an evidence map and a 2–3 page interdisciplinary plan: define the injury/context and uncertainty; identify safety issues; prioritize domain-specific evaluation; propose measurable function-centered goals; outline communication, referral, transitions and reassessment; cite current sources and label populations/scope. No real patient identifiers, images, records or copied case narratives.

unitMap.text: Foundations: injury mechanisms, classification and recovery
Acute-to-postacute continuity and referral
Disorders of consciousness and neurobehavioral recovery
Neurologic sequelae, imaging and secondary complications
Cognitive, communication and behavioral rehabilitation
Psychiatric sequelae and psychosocial recovery
Pain, sleep, fatigue and symptom persistence
Spasticity, mobility, tone, orthoses and procedures
Systemic, autonomic and medical complications
Functional assessment, outcome measurement and goal setting
Mild TBI, concussion and symptom-guided return
Adolescents, blast injury, equity and lifelong follow-up

topicGaps: This expansion adds 10 unique public recordings with observed durations. The original L001-L004 remain unknown-duration/unverified and are excluded; they have not been reclassified as hours.

Observed external specialty video totals 9.083889 hours (32702 seconds); 26.916111 hours of the 36-hour floor remain unfilled. Target minutes for planned episodes are not media and are never included in the ledger.
No complete publicly disclosed Spaulding institutional didactic/lecture catalogue was found. The MGB page describes clinical rotations and aims, not a full set of recorded teaching episodes.

Blueprint topics still lacking a verified full-length recording with equal board-level depth include disorders of consciousness, seizures/hydrocephalus, aphasia/dysphagia, spasticity/procedures, pain/sleep, systemic complications, neuropsychological test interpretation, blast injury, and detailed long-term management. Existing syllabus, readings, and scripted episodes do not close the video-hour gap.

The ten added recordings provide useful breadth but include older public-health webinars and introductory or interdisciplinary content; they do not collectively cover every 2026 ABPMR task statement or establish examination readiness.
Human clinician review was not performed. Source materials are not a substitute for current clinical protocols or supervised fellowship training.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

boardNames: American Board of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (ABPMR), Brain Injury Medicine subspecialty certification examination
American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology (ABPN), partner board in BIM certification
medical.boardStatus: ABPMR offers a distinct Brain Injury Medicine subspecialty certification; ABPMR states it has offered the certification in partnership with ABPN since 2014. This is not a primary specialty board and is not an automatic consequence of self-study or of listing a course. The 2026 ABPMR exam outline is the blueprint used here.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: As checked 2026-10-07, ABPMR says BIM exam applicants need a current, valid, unrestricted medical license and must be ABPMR diplomates in good standing or hold qualifying ABMS-board sports medicine subspecialty certification (ABOS orthopaedic sports medicine is excluded); for post-2022 examinations they must also complete 12 months of an ACGME-accredited BIM fellowship after residency and be recommended by the programme director. Verify current requirements directly with ABPMR/ABPN. This independent curriculum does not confer eligibility.

officialProgrammes.institution: Spaulding Rehabilitation Hospital (Mass General Brigham; Harvard Medical School-affiliated setting as described on MGB listing)
officialProgrammes.name: SRH Brain Injury Medicine Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official MGB listing calls it an approved ACGME-accredited 12-month physician fellowship in PM&R, with rotations at SRH, MGH and BWH; 3 months inpatient brain injury, 1 stroke, 1 LTACH, 1.5 outpatient neuro clinics, 1.5 MGH consults, 1 BWH consults/mild TBI clinics, 1.5 selective, and 2 weeks each neuro-radiology, neuro-ICU and research. Published rotation arithmetic totals 12 months. This is the single named Spaulding fellowship; the other sites are rotations, not separate institutional programmes in this item packet. The public listing is not a complete lecture catalogue.

medical.programmeSourceScope: This item is a clinical physician fellowship, not a generic directory category or a non-physician/research-only supplement. MGB’s own programme page identifies ACGME accreditation and fellowship clinical curriculum. It names SRH, MGH and BWH rotation sites, preserved here as exact institutional variants/sites; only one distinct official programme is listed in the packet. The curriculum page does not provide a complete set of lectures or establish a board examination; board status is independently verified with ABPMR.
sourceCaveats: The programme listing is a public overview; it does not expose an institutional lecture library or disclose all local didactic activities. No local curriculum details beyond the public MGB page are inferred.

ABPMR’s 2026 exam outline is effective for 2026 and should be checked again before use; board rules and exam dates can change. ABPMR is the primary administrative board and ABPN participates in the BIM certification partnership.
VA/DoD 2021 CPG is explicitly post-acute mild TBI; CDC source is pediatric mTBI. Do not use either beyond its specified population/time course without independent clinical justification.

Video search identified candidates, but direct YouTube metadata requests were blocked (429/403) and the NIH stateless page exposed title but no runtime/player. No outside runtime estimate was counted.
Case resources are links to publications/data, not reusable media. Free-to-view is not blanket permission to republish; no patient record, text, figure or image was copied.

Human clinical review is not performed. Independent education provides no Harvard/MGB/Spaulding/Johns Hopkins affiliation, accredited fellowship, licensure, board eligibility, procedural competence, certification, or guarantee of board performance.

topicGaps: This expansion adds 10 unique public recordings with observed durations. The original L001-L004 remain unknown-duration/unverified and are excluded; they have not been reclassified as hours.

Observed external specialty video totals 9.083889 hours (32702 seconds); 26.916111 hours of the 36-hour floor remain unfilled. Target minutes for planned episodes are not media and are never included in the ledger.
No complete publicly disclosed Spaulding institutional didactic/lecture catalogue was found. The MGB page describes clinical rotations and aims, not a full set of recorded teaching episodes.

Blueprint topics still lacking a verified full-length recording with equal board-level depth include disorders of consciousness, seizures/hydrocephalus, aphasia/dysphagia, spasticity/procedures, pain/sleep, systemic complications, neuropsychological test interpretation, blast injury, and detailed long-term management. Existing syllabus, readings, and scripted episodes do not close the video-hour gap.

The ten added recordings provide useful breadth but include older public-health webinars and introductory or interdisciplinary content; they do not collectively cover every 2026 ABPMR task statement or establish examination readiness.
Human clinician review was not performed. Source materials are not a substitute for current clinical protocols or supervised fellowship training.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 31-year-old adult is evaluated several weeks after a mild head injury for persistent symptoms. Which source is specifically intended to guide post-acute adult mTBI management?

options.text: CDC pediatric mTBI guidance
VA/DoD post-acute mTBI guideline
ACGME BIM requirements
NINDS general overview

practiceQuestions.rationale: The VA/DoD guideline is explicitly for management and rehabilitation of post-acute mild TBI; it includes an initial presentation algorithm >7 days and a persistent symptom algorithm. Applicability still depends on population and context.

practiceQuestions.stem: A school-age child with possible mild TBI is otherwise stable. Which approach is supported by CDC pediatric guidance?

options.text: Routine imaging to establish mTBI in every child
Use age-appropriate validated symptom scales and assess risk factors for prolonged recovery
Strict bed rest until all symptoms resolve
Clear the child for sport based only on normal imaging

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC recommends validated age-appropriate symptom scales, assessment of risk factors for prolonged recovery, symptom-tailored activity guidance, and does not recommend routine imaging solely to diagnose pediatric mTBI.

practiceQuestions.stem: After severe brain injury, an individual is awake at times but has no behavioral evidence of awareness across serial standardized assessments; reflex movement alone is present. What is the best conceptual next step?

options.text: Label the person minimally conscious based on reflex movement
Consider unresponsive wakefulness syndrome and reassess serially with attention to confounders
Diagnose brain death from behavior alone
Assume permanent prognosis from one exam

practiceQuestions.rationale: UWS describes wakefulness without evidence of awareness; diagnosis and prognosis require careful standardized serial assessment and exclusion of confounders. Reflexes alone do not demonstrate awareness.

practiceQuestions.stem: A rehabilitation patient has increasing tone and a thumb-in-palm posture that interferes with dressing. What should precede selecting an intervention?

options.text: Select injection solely from tone score
Clarify functional goals and distinguish spasticity from contracture/weakness, then discuss supervised options
Treat because any increased tone is harmful
Promise return to normal hand function

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ACGME requires functional assessment, goals, and proficiency in appropriate interventions; the problem must be tied to function and differential examination. Treatment is individualized and not guaranteed.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which set correctly matches the ABPMR 2026 BIM content outline domain weights?

options.text: CNS 30%, cognitive/behavioral 20%, psychiatric 15%, pain/sleep 15%, soft tissue/orthopedic 5%, systemic 15%
CNS 20%, cognitive 30%, psychiatric 15%, pain/sleep 10%, orthopedic 10%, systemic 15%
All six domains weighted equally
Acute trauma 50%, rehab 50%

practiceQuestions.rationale: These are the published 2026 outline percentages: CNS 30, cognitive/behavioral 20, psychiatric 15, pain/sleep 15, soft tissue/orthopedic 5, systemic 15.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with brain injury develops new worsening consciousness and focal weakness in a post-acute clinic. What is the best immediate reasoning priority?

options.text: Proceed with a routine fatigue handout
Urgently reassess for a new neurologic/medical complication and arrange appropriate escalation
Assume symptoms are expected post-concussion
Wait for formal neuropsychological testing

practiceQuestions.rationale: New neurologic deterioration is a safety red flag and requires urgent evaluation/escalation; routine rehabilitation pathways should not delay acute assessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner is asked to interpret neuropsychological testing for rehabilitation planning. Which statement best fits the ACGME competency?

options.text: Testing alone determines prognosis and disposition
Assess indications and interpret results alongside function and treatment planning
Every brain-injured patient needs identical testing
Testing is unnecessary if imaging is available

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME calls for proficiency in assessing indications for formal neuropsychological testing and interpreting results as they relate to treatment planning/prognostication, in context.

practiceQuestions.stem: An adolescent returns to school after concussion. Which planning element is most appropriate?

options.text: Ignore developmental needs because adult symptoms are similar
Coordinate gradual symptom-responsive return to learning/recreation and involve appropriate supports
Require complete symptom resolution before any non-sport activity
Treat return to school and return to sport as identical decisions

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME specifies adolescent emotional, behavioral, cognitive and developmental/school/recreation needs; CDC guidance supports gradual symptom-tailored return to non-sport activity after brief rest. Sport decisions require separate appropriate assessment.
practiceQuestions.domain: A CNS (30%); Etiology A sports mTBI

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with persistent dizziness after injury reports imbalance. What is the strongest initial educational reasoning approach?

options.text: Attribute all dizziness to vestibular injury
Characterize symptoms and function, consider differential/medical red flags, and coordinate targeted assessment
Order a single test that diagnoses every cause
Exclude sleep, medications and vision from assessment

practiceQuestions.rationale: Dizziness can have multiple neurologic, vestibular, visual, medication and systemic causes. ACGME expects evaluation of complications and functional assessment; targeted assessment is safer than presuming one cause.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about the Spaulding listing is accurate?

options.text: It is a self-study course accredited by ABPMR
It is described by MGB as an ACGME-accredited 12-month BIM fellowship with rotations at SRH, MGH and BWH
It awards board certification to anyone completing the public website curriculum
It is a research-only nonphysician training programme

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official MGB page identifies the programme as an ACGME-accredited 12-month fellowship and describes clinical rotations at Spaulding, MGH and BWH. Public course materials do not confer fellowship completion or certification.

topicGaps: Verified public recordings remain concentrated in cerebral palsy; the newly verified Seattle Children's spina bifida mobility lecture and two SMA rehabilitation recordings improve units 6 and 7 but do not provide complete coverage of pediatric SCI, DMD longitudinal care, neuromuscular examination, or current therapy-era standards. Both SMA recordings are 2020 uploads and require current-source review.

No counted accessible full lecture hours currently establish adequate coverage of pediatric orthopedics/limb difference, pediatric cancer rehabilitation, pediatric pain/POTS, genetic/rare disorders, and transitions/ethics. The 2025 AAPM&R catalog names several relevant offerings but its public listings did not establish no-login full playback plus player runtime; catalog/CME-course counts are not video hours.

boardNames: American Board of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (ABPMR) — Pediatric Rehabilitation Medicine subspecialty certification
medical.boardStatus: A separate ABPMR PRM subspecialty certification examination exists; the board page lists 280 questions in two 3.5-hour sections and an every-other-year schedule (checked 2026-10-07; next listed exam October 26, 2027). It is distinct from primary PM&R certification. This is a physician fellowship, not a generic directory label, research-only postdoctoral position, or non-physician supplement.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: ABPMR requires ABPMR diplomate status in good standing, an unrestricted qualifying medical license, and an accepted training route. The usual route is two years of ACGME-accredited PRM fellowship after PM&R residency; ABPMR specifies combined or consecutive-training alternatives. Self-study grants none of these. Hopkins public pages say one or two years depending on prior experience, while 2026 ACGME PRM requirements say 24 months and the KKI application page describes a two-year appointment. Resolve shorter-route details directly with the program and ABPMR; do not assume eligibility.

topicGaps: Verified public recordings remain concentrated in cerebral palsy; the newly verified Seattle Children's spina bifida mobility lecture and two SMA rehabilitation recordings improve units 6 and 7 but do not provide complete coverage of pediatric SCI, DMD longitudinal care, neuromuscular examination, or current therapy-era standards. Both SMA recordings are 2020 uploads and require current-source review.

No counted accessible full lecture hours currently establish adequate coverage of pediatric orthopedics/limb difference, pediatric cancer rehabilitation, pediatric pain/POTS, genetic/rare disorders, and transitions/ethics. The 2025 AAPM&R catalog names several relevant offerings but its public listings did not establish no-login full playback plus player runtime; catalog/CME-course counts are not video hours.

AACPDM and Spina Bifida Association guidance and open consensus articles support reading and original teaching scripts, not verified recording hours. Authored scripts remain scripted, unrendered and unprobed and contribute zero hours.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A four-month corrected-age infant has motor concerns. What plan is most consistent with early detection guidance?

options.text: Use an age-appropriate combined standardized assessment and imaging when feasible; interpret in context and support timely referral.
A single low screen score definitively diagnoses CP.
Wait until age two.
An MRI determines fixed prognosis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Combined age-appropriate evidence is favored; single tests do not determine diagnosis or future function.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child with CP has no hip pain. What is the best surveillance principle?

options.text: No monitoring until pain.
Clinical examination and radiographic surveillance complement each other; follow current pathway and individualized referral.
One normal radiograph ends follow-up.
Range of motion excludes displacement.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Hip displacement can be silent. The pathway is flagged for update, so verify current local schedule.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fluctuating postures interfere with seating in a child with CP. What is the best next step?

options.text: Assume spasticity and intervene immediately.
Assess dystonia and its functional impact, agree goals, and use shared decisions given conditional recommendations.
Assume fixed contracture without exam.
Treat only to normalize tone score.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AACPDM recommends dystonia assessment and goal-based shared decisions; evidence recommendations are conditional.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement matches 2025 CDC pediatric mTBI guidance?

options.text: Routine CT/MRI is required to diagnose mTBI.
Do not routinely image for diagnosis; use age-appropriate symptom scales and assess prolonged-recovery risks.
Strict bed rest until asymptomatic for two weeks.
Return to all activity immediately.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC discourages routine imaging for diagnosis and supports scales, risk evaluation and symptom-tailored return.

practiceQuestions.stem: A family requests universal high-intensity eccentric training in DMD. What is best?

options.text: Prescribe maximal resistance.
Coordinate individualized submaximal activity and monitor fatigue, contracture, fracture and cardiopulmonary context.
Stop all activity.
Track strength grade alone.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Care considerations support individualized multidisciplinary activity and caution against overexertion/high resistance.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the current US PRM board status?

options.text: No separate exam exists.
ABPMR offers a separate PRM subspecialty certification exam; this course grants no eligibility.
Any learner becomes eligible after quiz.
Fellowship completion automatically grants certification.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABPMR lists a distinct PRM examination with board-controlled training and license rules.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is a complete care map for a child with myelomeningocele?

options.text: Mobility and alignment alone.
Mobility, skin, bowel/bladder, orthopedics, self-management, psychosocial needs, prevention and transition.
Lesion level determines all participation.
Defer transition until adulthood.

practiceQuestions.rationale: SBA guidance spans lifespan preventive and participation domains; guidance is not legal standard.

practiceQuestions.stem: How long does the 2026 ACGME PRM specialty requirement specify?

options.text: 12 months for everyone.
24 months; clarify any institution-specific shorter route before assuming equivalence.
36 months minimum.
No length standard.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME states 24 months; Hopkins public webpages describe one or two years and need candidate-specific clarification.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is a good pediatric transition goal?

options.text: Automatic transfer at fixed age.
Plan with the person for autonomy, continuity, receiving-service responsibility, education and participation.
Stop preventive follow-up after growth.
Transfer without communication supports.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Lifespan care and coordination matter; local ages and policies vary.

practiceQuestions.stem: Can one ACGME milestone rating establish outside-learner certification or procedure competence?

options.text: Yes, Level 4 guarantees it.
No; milestones are developmental tools in accredited programs, not standalone credentialing; procedures require supervised training.
Yes, after self-study quiz.
Milestones replace board rules.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME limits intended use and warns against sole high-stakes use; procedure competence requires supervised training.
